Remco Evenepoel puts it all out there in a new long-form video interview with Specialized.

After a blockbuster first year with Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe, the Belgian star rates his season (“eight out of 10”), shares his take on the 2027 Tour de France route (he digs it), and offers intriguing insights into how his training has changed.

Released Thursday, the “Remco Evenepoel: Pursuit of Perfect” YouTube show is the latest in a flurry of off-season “rider does content” releases.

Tadej Pogačar got the red carpet treatment in not one, but two, feature documentaries , and Sepp Kuss broke YouTube with his “day in the life” video.

As a Specialized production, the conversation leans heavily on the rider’s “love” of his Tarmac and Shiv, and how he’s refining his position for 2027.

However, Evenepoel also speaks for the first time on the hottest topic of the past month: the 2027 Tour de France route.

The course for next year’s Tour de France has been labeled “anti-Pogačar” and “pro-Remco.”

Evenepoel is, of course, delighted with a parcours that offers the most time trialing in 15 years.

The four-time TT world champion can build a buffer in 71km against the clock that will buy him breathing room in the mountains.

“I’m very happy. If you see the most amount of TTs since 2012, that’s pretty good,” Evenepoel says in the video. “I would love it [the TTs] to be even a bit longer, but I’m very happy with what we’ve got.”

Evenepoel finished a distant second to Pogačar at the 2026 Tour de France.

However, next year offers him a slim chance to go one step better.

Evenepoel tells podcast host Ben Edwards that he and his entourage will spend winter figuring out how he can maximize his strengths for next summer’s showdown with Pog.

“I need to be able to bring my one-day TT performance into the grand tours,” Evenepoel says.

“In the world championships, I put a minute into [Filippo] Ganna, and at the Chrono des Nations, I put two minutes into [Jay] Vine. If I can bring those performances into the grand tours, I’d gain even more.

“What is now my ‘very good’ must now become the standard,” he continues. “Over winter we’ll have to see how and when, and why we can or can’t do that. I’m sure with all the knowledge the team and my little crew around me have, and with my own experience, that we can find that.”

Evenepoel adds that he hopes to devise an energy management plan so that he can peak for his key stages of the Tour and play defense elsewhere.

“We need to make a strategy to come into those TTs fresh and really use them to see what time they will bring,” he says.

Maybe Evenepoel’s new training framework will help.

In the video, the 26-year-old discusses how Tim Heemskerk – the former coach of Jonas Vingegaard – revolutionized his approach to training.

The Dutch staffer joined Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe mid-season and brought a new data-driven approach to workouts.

“Tim really wanted all sorts of inside information – sleeping metrics, weight, HRV, all that stuff. He wanted it every single day,” Evenepoel says.

“He wanted it first thing in the morning so he could see how the values were overnight. Then he could adapt something [for the coming workout] if necessary,” Evenepoel says. “That was never a way I’ve been thinking.”

The video runs to almost an hour in length, but it’s well worth a watch. What else are you going to do now there’s no road racing to binge on?

Watch the full show on Specialized’s YouTube channel.

Vacek, inset, watched as Ayuso struggled in 2026. (Photo: Getty Images)

Mathias Vacek might not be a household name yet, but he’s a rising star at budding super team Lidl-Trek .

And he clearly isn’t afraid to speak his mind.

In an interview with MARCA , the Czech rider offered a candid assessment of Juan Ayuso’s first season with the team, saying the Spanish star fell short of what he was expecting.

“To be honest, I expected more from him. He started good with the win in the Algarve, and it looked promising, but throughout the season I had the feeling something is missing,” Vacek told MARCA . “He was good, but not at the top like we were used to. I think everyone could see it.”

Ayuso moved to Lidl-Trek in 2026 after a blockbuster transfer and a controversial split with UAE Emirates-XRG. He wanted more freedom, and Lidl-Trek offered him a juicy contract and the chance to headline its grand tour ambitions.

After a hot start to beat Paul Seixas at the Volta ao Algarve , his spring came off the rails. He crashed out of Paris-Nice while in the leader’s jersey and then abandoned Itzulia Basque Country with illness.

Vacek, who made his Tour debut this summer, said he saw warning signs as the Tour approached .

“At the Sierra Nevada training camp, he had allergy problems, he went back home to Andorra, and he started training, but you could feel that something was going on. I don’t know whether it was mental or what,” Vacek said.

“I don’t want to say something I don’t know, but that’s my feeling,” he said. “In the end, at the Tour, you could see he was cooked, and Skjelmose was better than him. Definitely, for me when we signed him, I expected him to be like he was in the earlier years.”

Vacek was also quick to say that Ayuso can fly when everything clicks and stressed he was only sharing his observations, not criticizing his teammate.

“If he’s really good, if he’s on a wave, he can be top, he can also follow Pogi,” he said. “With these guys, when mentally something is wrong, if something wrong or a little detail is missing, they lose the confidence a bit.”

Vacek was equally honest about his own season.

The 24-year-old is emerging as a potential classics powerhouse , but his spring campaign fizzled. He didn’t hit the top 20 all spring and later saved his season with two stage wins and the GC at the ZLM Tour.

What happened? He says he overloaded too soon in an early season build in southern Spain.

“It was a season of ups and downs. Starting at the beginning, the classics went badly for me because I was tired. I started training quite early, and in Spain, with the good weather, you get into shape in three or four weeks,” Vacek told MARCA . “I got carried away with training so early. By the classics, when it really mattered, I was exhausted.”

A reset and an altitude camp helped turn things around. Vacek finished third overall at the Tour de Suisse, then completed his Tour debut by helping teammate Mads Pedersen secure the green jersey.

At the Tour de Suisse, simply staying close to Tadej Pogačar counted for more.

“When I was able to follow Pogačar on a stage of the Tour de Suisse. I think that was something even bigger than a victory for me, because there aren’t many riders capable of following him,” he said. “That was definitely the high point. And the worst moment, without doubt, was the crash in Montréal where I broke my nose.

“That’s cycling. There are always bad moments, but if you know you’re giving everything and committing 100 percent, you know the good moments will eventually come.”

Lidl-Trek brass clearly more upside and Vacek is signed through 2029.

Some see him taking over classics leadership from Pedersen when the big Dane retirees.

“Yes, I’ve had several one-on-one conversations with Mads. He’s a very honest person and tells you things exactly as he feels them,” Vacek told MARCA . “He has told me clearly that I’m one of the riders who will take over when he retires.”

Already four seasons in the WorldTour, Vacek says he’s not a carbon-copy of the marauding Dane, but admits he takes inspiration from the former world champion.

“I want to follow a clear path, try to be like him, and achieve the same victories. I’m a slightly different type of rider because I climb better, but I want to follow in his footsteps,” Vacek said.

“Everything I can learn from him now benefits me. I feel I’m gradually getting closer to his level, so I hope to be there soon if everything goes well.”

He’s obviously already taken one lesson to heart about being a leader — say what you think.

Another Pogačar documentary drops this week and dives into his roots. (Photo: Gruber Images)

Long before he was dominating the Tour de France, Tadej Pogačar was spending his birthday money on socks and sunglasses.

That’s according to POG1: The Making of a Legend , a new documentary that drops this week from Colnago Cultura.

The latest in a flurry of fresh Pogačar content, the documentary follows the Slovenian’s evolution from an unknown kid to a global phenomenon.

The director uses interviews with his parents, his partner Urška Žigart, longtime mentor Andrej Hauptman, teammates and ex-pros to tell the story of his rise to Tour de France dominance.

The documentary premieres Friday on Colnago’s YouTube channel and it’s free in every country.

Velo has only seen a few snippets, but this documentary dives into Pogačar’s origin story with new details and anecdotes.

Pogačar’s father recounts how his son followed his older brother into football and then cycling. Once the bike took over, it was clear to his parents that Little Pogi was obsessed.

“As soon as he started it became the only thing in the world that he was interested in. Cycling, cycling,” he said. “All the money he got for a birthday or something he would spend on socks or sunglasses. Nothing else interested him anymore.”

Pogačar has since emerged as the most dominant male rider of this century, and even Eddy Merckx has admitted the Slovenian could end up the best ever to race a bike.

The documentary traces his backstory and highlights a telling moment from one of Pogačar’s earliest races.

Hauptman, now a sports director at UAE Emirates-XRG, recalls arriving midway through a youth race in Ljubljana in 2012 and spotting a small rider apparently struggling several hundred meters behind the group.

“I came in the middle of the race, and one of our riders was really a few hundred meters behind the group. I spoke with the organizer, and said, ‘Why don’t we help this small guy to catch the group?’” Hauptman said. “He said, ‘Who? You mean this one? No, no, he will win. He overlapped the whole peloton.’”

“When you’re a kid, you just have fun. You don’t think too much about the future. I realized maybe the second year of juniors and U23 that I could go into the WorldTour and race the biggest races,” Pogačar said. “The first race I started, I finished last. I didn’t care. I just had such a good time.”

UAE signed him before he won the 2018 Tour de l’Avenir, and the trophies have been piling up ever since.

POG1 arrives a week after another documentary from Eurosport/TNT called Anatomy of a GOAT .

That film focused more on the physiology behind Pogačar’s success, revealing some interesting numbers on his heart rate, sleep scores, and heart rate variability from Whoop data.

Velo has seen only selected preview clips of the Colnago film, but it appears to focus more on his family, childhood, and personality, and traces the foundation of how Pogačar became the world No. 1.

Both documentaries come as the 28-year-old recovers from his devastating crash that ended his Vuelta a España and kept him out of the road worlds and Il Lombardia.

He’s already back to training and is set to reveal his 2027 racing calendar at UAE’s team camp in Spain next month.

Peter Sagan's final team TotalEnergies will keep racing after the arrival of a new sponsor, but there's no room for Roglič. (Photo: Michael Steele/Getty Images)

TotalEnergies — the second-tier French team where Peter Sagan ended his career — is saved by the bell as teams and riders are getting nervous as 2026 winds down.

Team manager Jean-René Bernaudeau revealed Tuesday that XEFI, a French IT company, committed to three years to keep the long-running team in the peloton.

With just weeks before winter team camps, the announcement went down to the wire to meet registration deadlines and keep riders under contract.

“It’s late, there was pressure, there was anticipation, that much we understand. But today, we savor this feeling of peace and confidence all the more,” sport director Stéphane Heulot told L’Equipe .

Heulot said the team will see a mix of veterans and rising talent for 2027, mostly French, but with more international tilt in the coming season.

Is there room for Primoz Roglič , the superstar Slovenian who is still hunting for a deal? Probably not.

“I would say that today the roster is almost complete. A shock transfer? I don’t know who we could talk about today. Roglič maybe? But honestly, that’s not something we have on the table,” he said. “I don’t want to do a publicity stunt like some teams have done when they don’t actually have the means to hire him.”

The deal saves the team from the edge of oblivion. TotalEnergies confirmed the end of its long-running sponsorship with the team, but appears to be remaining in cycling with partnership with Netcompany-Ineos.

After flirting with international riders like Sagan — who raced his final two seasons with the team — and Edvald Boasson Hagen, the team pivoted back to its French roots the past few years. It won a Tour de France stage in 2024 with Antony Turgis and provided a pipeline for more French riders to start the Tour.

The team was founded in 2000 and has raced the Tour every year since.

Fans will recognize the different names over the years, from Bonjour, Brioches La Boulangère, Bouygues Télécom, Europcar, Direct Énergie, and TotalEnergies, but this has been Bernaudeau’s baby.

The late-hour save is good news for French cycling, which is facing the same problems of rising costs while trying to compete against a few elite super teams at the top of the pyramid.

Coming out of 2026, no major WorldTour teams are facing imminent closure, but there are a few teams in the lower ranks that look to be closing.

France’s St Michel-Auber93 — a modest team from a Parisian suburb that raced a few Tours over the years — is shutting down its long-running men’s that dates back to the 1990s. Management will pivot toward backing the women’s team and hope for a Tour de France Femmes invitation in 2027.

Hitec Products, a women’s Norwegian Continental team, confirmed its shutting down at the end of this season, citing difficulties to get into major races.

Two more second-tier men’s teams that played out-sized roles are also shutting at the end of 2026.

Team Flanders-Baloise, with its DNA dating back to the 1990s, is folding after the Flemish government withdrew key public funding. Long a fixture in the classics, the team was a “talent farm” for budding Belgian riders to make the jump to the WorldTour.

Thomas De Gendt, Sep Vanmarcke, Victor Campenaerts, Oliver Naesen, and Yves Lampaert all did stints with the team over the years.

Kern Pharma, the Spanish ProTeam since 2020, is also restructuring for 2027 after the longtime pharmaceutical company did not extend its sponsorship. Riders like Pablo Castrillo, Roger Adrìa and Raúl García Pierna all raced on the team before bouncing to the WorldTour.

Riders have been told they’re free to find new teams and the squad could continue at a lower level next season.

The Slovenian showed up this week in Taiwan, but there’s still no confirmed team for the four-time Vuelta a España champion.

The 37-year-old parted ways with Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe after three season, and it remains uncertain if there will be a closing-hour deal.

Contract talks with several teams, including Visma-Lease a Bike, Unibet Rose Rockets, Pinarello-Q36.5, and Lotto-Intermarché, have all apparently collapsed.

Roglič — once of cycling’s “Big Four” — remains ambivalent about his future and even whether he wants to continue racing.

He still finished second at the Vuelta a España and earned nearly 1,000 UCI points in 2026, which would be valuable to teams chasing a WorldTour license, but a reported $2 million asking price might have to come down if he wants to find a deal this late in the season.

It might be true, but the argument has got a flaw.

Speaking on the latest episode of his Watts Occurring podcast, Thomas drew the popular comparison between Paul Seixas and Tadej Pogačar .

The team Ineos long-timer and former Tour de France winner felt there’s only one winner, and he’s French.

“It was unreal from him this year. Fair play,” Thomas said of Seixas. “What can you say?

“He’s better than Pog when Pog was that age,” Thomas said. “It’s not just the wins, but how he seems. He just seems more advanced, more developed.”

Seixas has been spoken of with the reverence typically reserved for Pogačar throughout his incredible breakout season.

The spindly Frenchman tore apart Itzulia Basque Country and La Fléche Wallonne. He finished fourth at the Tour de France as a debuting 19-year-old. He became the youngest winner of Il Lombardia at age 20.

Thomas was adamant when speaking to Luke Rowe – who works as sport director on Seixas’ team at Decathlon CMA-CGM – that 2026 marked the arrival of cycling’s next dominator.

“It’s going to be an exciting few years for him and for France and for your team. He’s just going to continue to improve,” Thomas said.

Cycling hasn’t seen such a prodigious talent since the arrival of … well, Pogačar. They’re two phenoms, seven years apart.

But is it fair to draw parallels between their careers?

Pogačar’s countryman and long-time teammate Domen Novak would argue “no.”

Speaking earlier this March with Sportal , Novak highlighted an important distinction between the two: their teenage regimens.

“The guy is really very good,” Novak said of Seixas. ‘Everyone compares him to Tadej; they want to put him next to him, and considering his age, he is even better than Tadej was.

“But you need to know something else,” Novak told Sportal . “As far as I know Tadej, he didn’t do any altitude training in those early years. He was racing for the Gusto Ljubljana team. I can say that he won his first Tour while eating pizza, drinking beer and playing PlayStation.”

Novak was likely pouring on the hyperbole, but he has a point.

Seixas only turned 20 in September, but is already one of the most buttoned-down, hyper-professional athletes in the entire peloton.

He locked himself into a high-altitude training camp away from family and friends for two months in the winter, pulled a ridiculous three-week block to prepare for the Tour, and berates himself for every rookie racing error.

He’s got high standards and higher expectations.

There’s no doubt that his life is ruled by bathroom scales, HRV scores, and watt-per-kilo targets.

By contrast, 20-year-old Pogačar carried puppy fat and unabashed naiveté into his debut year with UAE Emirates-XRG.

In 2019, high-carb fueling and HRV tracking were pipedreams and disc brakes were for revolutionaries.

Not that such Stone Age approaches stopped Pogačar from winning the Tour of California and blasting to third on his grand tour debut at the Vuelta a España, of course.

Novak questioned the sustainability of Seixas’ approach when he spoke with Sportal . We won’t find out if his fears are well-founded for a decade.

Meanwhile, Thomas said on his podcast that only burnout or boredom will slow Pogačar’s stampede across pro cycling.

“Pog’s still improving. He was the best Pog this year than he has been,” Thomas said, caveating that the 28-year-old Pogačar of 2026 is without doubt better than the 20-year-old Seixas.

“He’s unique, don’t get me wrong, Pog,” Thomas continued.

“Mentally, if he can still commit and do everything right, he can keep improving until he’s 35,” he said.

If Thomas is right and Seixas and Pogačar both keep improving, we could have another seven years to argue over how they compare.

(Photo: OSCAR DEL POZO/AFP via Getty Images)

Sepp Kuss could just be the dude next door who’s good at riding bikes.

In a new “Day in the Life” video, Kuss walks viewers through the boring mundanity of his life at home in Andorra during the off-season.

As you’d expect from Colorado’s fan favorite, it’s all pretty chill.

There are cookies for breakfast, grand tour trophies gathering dust in hallways, and a man-cave cluttered with bike bits.

His lifestyle seems hilariously lackadaisical. His home has few trappings of an elite athlete who’s likely getting paid seven figures.

The high-end Porsche parked in the garage is the one giveaway that this is not your normal guy.

Visma-Lease a Bike released its “Day in the Life” mini-doc this week after its long-signed American star blasted through one of his best seasons yet.

This year, Kuss rode all three grand tours in the season for the second time in his career.

The “Eagle of Durango” won a stage at the Giro d’Italia, nearly won two stages at the Tour de France, and made a late surge for fifth overall at the Vuelta a España.

Few riders dare take on three grand tours in a season, but Kuss made it look easy.

In the video, Kuss says the program keeps life how he likes it – simple and stress-free.

“I’ve been able to be home a lot between all three grand tours [this year], and that makes a big difference,” he says.

“Mentally it was easier than a normal season, because you have really concrete blocks and concrete goals. Between that, it’s a pretty simple routine and easy living,” he says.

Kuss’ young family is no doubt front of mind when he structures his calendar.

His Spanish-born wife, Noemi, and two-year-old daughter, Martina, feature heavily in the documentary, and Sepp is in all-out dad-mode throughout.

He plays with his daughter, takes her on a bike ride, and helps Noemi feed her bits of cake.

Kuss is pro cycling’s ultimate dad next door.

He’s just a 32-year-old dude who casually enjoys bikes, baking, and crushing Tour de France climbs at a billion watts per kilo.

And yes, you read that right, Kuss appears to be a passionate baker – one with a sweet tooth.

Food and food-prep feature heavily in the show.

There’s no controversial kimchi-and-gnocchi concoction like the one favored by Matteo Jorgenson, but there are some interesting insights.

Kuss reveals a refreshingly casual attitude to food that’s careful but far from restrictive.

“Every morning has to start with cookies or a cake,” Kuss says as he cuts the final slices of what looks like a huge home bake.

“We usually try to go for something more homemade, but a lot of the time it’s just normal cookies from the grocery store. Not a perfect diet,” he smiles.

The waifish climber adds that he barely restricts and allows a little luxury, all year round.

It’s no doubt all carefully considered and meticulously tracked on a food app, but Kuss doesn’t appear overly concerned about optimizing his W/Kg ratio in the depths of off-season.

“My diet is never so strict. It stays pretty much the same all year,” he says. “We eat well, but there’s nothing that I don’t eat in the off-season versus in the normal season.

“There are always some chips in the pantry,” he adds.

Kuss’s “aww shucks” character and boyish charm have made him one of the darlings of the pro peloton.

He’s well liked by his colleagues, loved by the media (he’ll rarely say no to an interview), and adored by fans.

Kuss’ reluctant stardom is epitomized as the camera follows him through his home.

Bike mementos are casually scattered in random places and seemingly displayed out of obligation.

The huge wine bottle he won at the Giro d’Italia is gathering dust in a doorway.

His Vuelta a España stage-winner’s plaque sits on a shelf in the garage alongside a handmade #GCKuss token and a bunch of random bike oils.

“You either have a trophy room, or you find the nice ones to put somewhere, but …,” Kuss says with a shy shrug.

Kuss’ garage also functions as a bike store and workshop.

Unlike the many pros who can barely change a tire, Kuss is teaching himself the art of bike maintenance as a “hobby mechanic.”

Oh, and the special-edition red Cervélo that Kuss rode on the final stage of his career-crowning ride at the Vuelta?

Lost in a mess of a half-dozen bikes hanging in a rack.

What did you expect? A pride-of-place position hanging on the wall of his lounge?

Kuss is one of the greatest U.S. racers of his generation.

He became the first North American to win a grand tour in a decade when he won the 2023 Vuelta a España, and is one of the few active pros to have taken a stage at all three of cycling’s three-week races.

But Kuss often seems embarrassed by his own success.

It should be considered a miracle then, that his Vuelta a España winner’s trophy has made it out of the cupboard.

The large circular prize he was awarded in 2023 stands on a cabinet in a dark corner of his home.

And that low-key position should be considered progress.

Last year, Kuss revealed in a Sigma Sport video that his prestigious trophy wasn’t proudly standing triumphant in a cabinet, but tucked deep in the back of a cupboard.

Visma’s recently retired Dutch stalwart Robert Gesink makes a cameo appearance in the video when he meets Kuss for a coffee.

The 40-year-old believes Kuss’ innate zen has bought him longevity.

“The biggest strength of Sepp is that he found the really nice balance,” Gesink says. “He does everything right, he weighs his food, he does his training correctly, but he has the right balance and doesn’t overdo it.

“If you can keep that balance and find a way that works for you and you can sustain that level, then you can keep growing,” Gesink continues.

“That’s how you can build such a long and successful career if you find your own way to make that sustainable and not lose yourself straight away in all these little details.”

Kuss is currently out in L.A. visiting Cervélo HQ with several Visma-Lease a Bike teammates.…

Athletes are going off-sponsor to get lactate fuel. (Photo: Gruber Images)

Lactate fueling arrived with such wild hype at the Tour de France that it’s been forced undercover.

ExoLactate has launched an “unbadged” version of its revolutionary gels to meet a surge in demand from athletes who want to tap into the lactate boom, without causing a kerfuffle with team sponsors.

The pioneering Basque brand revealed its exclusive all-silver packaging on Instagram this weekend.

“ExoLactate Gel is used by elite-level athletes to fuel performance at the pinnacle of endurance sports. Sponsorship commitments mean many of these top-ranked ‘testers’ endorse ExoLactate anonymously,” reads the post .

“Now available is ExoLactate Classified, unbranded ExoLactate products, for elite application only.”

The launch of these secretive silver packets is a telling sign.

There’s some serious FOMO around what could be the next superfuel of elite endurance.

The secretive arrival of a first wave of lactate fuels at this summer’s Tour de Franc e was met with a swell of hype, intrigue and suspicion.

Exogenous lactate provides a third fuel source that works alongside the carbohydrates, glucose and fructose, and supercharges metabolism. We wrote a deeper explainer of how lactate fueling works, and why it’s not really “the enemy” here.

Insiders believe lactate fueling has the potential to be as big a breakthrough as the carbohydrate revolution or carbon-plated running super shoes.

But at present, the supply of these next-gen gels and drink mixes is limited.

ExoLactate and Enervit – the partner of Tadej Pogačar ‘s team UAE Emirates-XRG – are leading the boom.

Pogačar was guzzling Enervit’s lactate gel mix en route to his fifth Tour de France title this summer.

ExoLactate was supplying one of the Slovenian’s rival Tour teams, albeit under a strict anonymity clause.

ExoLactate and its “From Lab to Field” research group are also deeply embedded in professional trail running. The gels were used with wild success and podium results at the “Super Bowl” of ultra running, UTMB (Ultra-Trail du Mont Blanc).

Meanwhile, the rest of the carbohydrate-focused sport nutrition industry is scrambling to keep up with these lactate first-movers.

At present, only a small handful of derivative, scientifically dubious products are available.

But demand has skyrocketed since the summer.

Approval from Pogačar, proof-of-concept at the biggest bike and trail races in the world, and fear of missing out have made lactate gels a must-have.

ExoLactate founder Aitor Viribay told Velo that he experienced so much interest in his product – a gel that combines 5g lactate and 40g carbohydrate – that it was a no-brainer to launch “Classified.”

The anonymized packaging allows athletes to stray from sponsor commitments, undetected.

No taped-over gels or secretly decanted drink mixes necessary.

“We’ve had so many elites asking for a way to use lactate. And we wanted to support them because we believe in how much potential it has to change performance,” Viribay told Velo .

“But of course elites have their contracts with Maurten or Amacx or Science in Sport or whoever, and we respect that,” he said. “We don’t want to fight with those companies. But the athletes want to use lactate, and they are looking for ways to make it happen.”

Viribay – a former nutritionist at Ineos Grenadiers and the current head of performance at the Solomon running team – said the service honors ExoLactate’s two-way relationship with the elite.

The brand loses revenue and exposure through the service, but gains commitment, feedback, and trust in a fledgling product that’s still evolving.

“There was demand for the service from elites, so we opened the service,” Viribay said. “You have to apply and demonstrate that you have a commitment, and then we can sell to you with that unbranded packaging.

“We don’t make any more money selling the gels this way. These teams and athletes get special discounts,” Viribay continued. “But this is more a service for them because we want to work with them. We are born for elites. We are happy to help them because our goal is not just marketing.”

The professionalization and monetization of pro cycling means every nook and cranny of the sport, and the teams that compete within it, is sponsored.

In the past decades, team partnerships have exploded beyond bikes, helmets, and clothing to include nutrition, leisurewear, recovery products, and even bedding.

Contracts demand athletes “use” – or at least, are seen to be using – products from their team’s invested provider.

But in a sport where the margins are so fine, that’s not always what happens in practice.

Teams commonly ran blacked-out, off-sponsor wheels, saddles, and occasionally bike frames through the 2000s and 2010s. If something was faster, and a team could find a way to use it, they’d make it happen.

A more recent leveling in the bike-tech landscape has made this less of a “thing” in the Pogačar era.

However, off-sponsor pivots remain common in nutrition, where palatability and stomach-compatibility are unique to the individual and essential for success.

And in some cases, products are simply too good to miss.

Maurten’s carbohydrate hydrogels generated so much hype when they helped spark the carbohydrate revolution that the brand foreshadowed ExoLactate by selling unbranded products.

Close to a decade later, Maurten remains a top choice for the sporting elite.

Velo spoke to several WorldTour trainers and nutritionists who are skeptical of products that still lack published research and remain so novel in their use.

Viribay accepted the reluctance when he spoke to Velo . However, he was hopeful that the imminent publication of external studies will persuade the naysayers.

The Basque scientist also suggested the lactate curious more than match the skeptics.…

Poundland and its 11,000 employees are hopeful that the retailer's impending collapse can be delayed to allow time for a last-minute rescue deal.

The discount chain has been edging towards administration after being blocked by its owners from accessing cash in its bank accounts.

A deadline to secure a buyer for the business is set to expire at midnight, but sources close to the situation have told the BBC that they expect more time will be given, thanks to the release of £10m in funding.

A committee of MPs is set to question Gordon Brothers, Poundland's US owners, on Wednesday following accusations that the investment firm hopes to profit from selling off Poundland's 600 stores and stock piecemeal.

Gordon Brothers - which bought the chain for just £1 last year - is accused of forcing that outcome by restricting Poundland's access to available cash needed to restock stores and pay wages and rent, ahead of the crucial Christmas trading period.

The investment firm has denied the claims.

But pressure remains on Poundland's owners after a takeover bid was rejected. The decision prompted calls for answers from politicians, including Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

About £50m had been frozen by Gordon Brothers, the BBC understands, meaning Poundland bosses were unable to restock shelves across its 600 shops.

However, sources close to the matter told the BBC on Tuesday that a release of £10m by its owners, while "small in the scale of things" could help at least postpone the chain's collapse while a longer term solution was explored.

The 10-day moratorium to protect Poundland from its creditors expires on Thursday, but if there is a prospect of a solvent deal, the deadline could be extended.

Views on the chain's performance differ between those running operations and the owners.

Poundland boss Barry Williams told staff last week that like-for-like sales, which exclude new store openings, were up 11.4%. The sales period included Halloween, but Williams said this was £1.5m ahead of budget.

He added the business made a profit of £18.1m in the year to September, which was a "strong recovery" from the previous year where there were losses of £68m.

However, Gordon Brothers has painted a different picture, saying the chain remains "challenged and vulnerable to any potential downturn in future trading".

There has been interest from the likes of Poundstretcher, Tesco and B&M in picking up Poundland stores which could mean continuing employment for workers in the event the chain is broken up and sold off in chunks.

The main issue is whether a piecemeal sale would protect more jobs than a buyer willing to keep Poundland as a national chain.

Randy Gail Sperino was last seen alive on the evening of 9 November 1993, as she was getting into a pickup truck in Granite City, Illinois.

The 34-year-old's body was found hours later in a field nearby, the victim of blunt force trauma.

The identity of her killer was a mystery. DNA evidence found at the crime scene was tested against standard law enforcement databases, but no matches were found.

For three decades, investigators from the Madison County Sheriff's Office chased leads and interviewed hundreds of people as they attempted to identify the perpetrator.

The case looked like it would remain one of more than 250,000 unsolved homicides in the US.

Then, last year, detectives tried a fresh approach. They sent genetic evidence to Othram, a Houston-based company that uses DNA technology to help identify the perpetrators in cold and current crime cases.

The Madison County detectives had been inspired by investigative genetic genealogy techniques used to identify the Golden State Killer, Joseph James DeAngelo, back in 2018. In that case, an investigative team constructed a family tree to help identify the killer.

They were able to do so thanks to DNA data that relatives had provided to commercial databases, similar to consumer ancestry platforms.

Unlike traditional forensic DNA testing, which generally relies on a direct comparison between evidence and a known person, investigative genetic genealogy can identify distant genetic relatives of an unknown individual.

Othram set about applying this technique to track down Sperino's killer. While the killer's own DNA profile wasn't available, profiles submitted by his extended relatives allowed the company to identify a male family member.

"That lead broke the case open," said Captain Tim Lawrence of Madison County Sheriff's Office, which was responsible for investigating the crime.

It was a crucial clue that led the detectives to Albert "Buddy" Zigler, 70, who then confessed to the murder. He was charged in May this year.

Wes Sperino, Gail's son, said at a press conference: "I finally get closure and I finally know who did this."

The technique that led detectives to Zigler is credited with revolutionising how forensic cases are solved.

It has been highly successful in helping solve cases involving unidentified human remains and identifying suspects in longstanding investigations.

Othram claims it has helped solve thousands of cases. The company's chief executive David Mittelman likens investigative genetic genealogy to a GPS system: "The DNA profile is the GPS signal and it says 'you belong here.' But to understand where 'here' is, you need a map."

Public records, obituaries, and census data build that map so Othram's scientists can establish how different family trees connect.

However, Mittelman is quick to point out that DNA technology can only go so far before "a cascade of investigative steps" are needed.

DNA science isn't the only technology that are helping detectives solve cold cases.

One of the challenges facing detectives on major cases investigations like the hunt for Sperino's killer is the sheer amount of evidence they dig up.

Officers investigating Sperino's murder realised AI could help them wade through the mountains of evidence they had accumulated since 1993.

They used a platform called Centerline AI, from Florida software company CentralSquare, to analyse more than 2,000 pages of records and identify evidence for the DNA testing that helped to break the case.

The AI helped them reconstruct timelines and organise witness information. "It's so much easier than having a detective have to read through 2,000 pages," Lawrence says. His team could interact with the AI like a chat bot.

This also helped when it came to interviewing Zigler after they had tracked him down. Detectives were able to ask questions of the AI to help "figure out if Zigler was being truthful", says Lawrence.

But the technology is "only as good as the investigator," says the captain. There comes a point, he says, "where you leave the technology behind and you have to go track people down and talk to them."

Investigative genetic genealogy has its limitations too. Mittelman says: "It can't solve every case. If you have no DNA, you can't really use this technique."

"But this technique is a lot more powerful and a lot more likely to yield identities than having to rely on the chance that you find a match somewhere in a database," he adds.

While firms like Othram only use ancestry platforms where users have provided consent for law enforcement matching, there remain some concerns about the ethical implications of using this data.

"There are significant privacy concerns," says Denise Syndercombe Court, professor of forensic genetics at King's College London. While one person may have opted in to their DNA being used, genetic relatives may not have given consent.

A lack of funding is another hurdle. Mittelman says: "Every law enforcement agency wants to do it. There's just not a lot of funding for it."

Sometimes cases are funded through donations or crowdfunding. Othram operates a website listing cases that members of the public can help fund.

While investigative genetic genealogy has been adopted in countries such as Sweden, Denmark and Australia, it is not yet used in the UK. The Home Office is conducting a study to consider whether it should be adopted in the UK but did not respond to a request for comment.

The UK is already in a strong position, says Syndercombe Court. "We have such an efficient DNA database that if you can get any DNA out of a crime scene, you've got over a 65% chance of putting a name to that person, which is enormously powerful," she says.

Rising costs could force the cider industry to reduce their reliance on British-grown apples, according to several well-established businesses.

Higher alcohol duty, energy bills and packaging costs are making it harder to stay profitable, according to a producer in Somerset.

The government said it was supporting the sector by increasing the value of Small Producer Relief, which provides lower alcohol duty rates for some smaller and medium-sized producers.

Matilda Temperley, director of Burrow Hill farm near Martock, said it would be a "tragedy" to stop using its own apples due to climbing costs.

Temperley, whose farm has been growing apples for 300 years, said recent increases had added to pressures already facing the industry, adding at 6% alcohol, their traditional cider is taxed at a higher rate than mass produced cider.

Gritters out for the first time this autumn

No radical change after nationalisation, GWR says

"By next February, we will have seen a 61% increase in tax on our standard 50cl bottles," Temperley claimed.

She welcomed the rise in Small Producers Relief but said other mounting costs outweighed it.

"We've got huge, energy costs, then almost a 90% increase in tax costs since 2020."

"The thing that will happen is that if you're a big cider maker, you're going to look to cut your costs and the only way to cut costs is to stop using British apples," she said.

"That's a real tragedy because cider should be made from these beautiful orchards".

Isaac Stell, a financial analyst at Wealth Club in Bristol, said that having pledged not to raise the main rates of income tax, national insurance or VAT for working people, the recent budget focused on other areas to "help plug the fiscal hole."

He said producers were also dealing with higher employer National Insurance contributions and increases in the minimum wage.

"Inevitably, some of those additional costs will find their way through to the pubs, clubs and restaurants that producers supply, and ultimately to an already squeezed consumer. "

The Showerings family, known for producing Babycham, has been making drinks in Shepton Mallet for more than 14 generations.

"Our business has grown a lot in the last ten years - we've gone from having 80 employees to around 350 now," the firm's managing director Matthew Showering said.

"We've had a good couple of years, we're making drinks that are popular and growing."

While acknowledging rising costs, Showering said he would rather see less government intervention.

"We don't want any help from the government, we'd rather they keep out of things as much as possible."

Matt Gillett from Tricky's Cider in Low Ham said the size of his operation means he will be eligible for the Small Producer Relief but adds he will not see a huge benefit as the Alcohol Duty is a "fairly substantial" part of his monthly outgoings.

Gillett remains optimistic, and said he would not consider importing pulp or concentrate to cut costs.

"We are a craft producer here in Somerset and are proud of the fact we take from local orchards, traditional orchards, and use the fruit that is available here in this county."

A spokesperson for the Treasury said: "The cider industry makes a vital contribution to our rural economy and communities, and cider continues to benefit from significantly lower duty rates than other alcoholic drinks.

"But we know the industry is facing continued pressures, which is why the Budget provides additional support by cutting costs for pubs and bars that are vital customers for the industry and poured pints continue to benefit from draught relief."

Jensen Huang has the air of the late Steve Jobs about him. I have interviewed both, and the up-close charisma - and occasionally scratchy genius - is shared.

Both sported a signature item of black clothing, although Huang opts for a leather jacket rather than the Apple founder's turtle neck.

Both are innovators revered in the tech world. However, Huang is now being investigated over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy .

Everything you have heard about Artificial Intelligence (AI) over the past few months - good, bad, revolutionary and catastrophic - is dependent on having the most powerful frontier AI models.

In turn they depend on the most powerful microchips, and for years that has been this very company, Nvidia, led by Huang, and his technology rooted in repurposed games graphics and the manufacturing prowess of Taiwan.

Names such as Gracehopper, Vera and Rubin mean almost nothing to the public, but are the names of chips powering the creation of AI models transforming the world.

I met Huang as he held court with reporters and offered words of encouragement for the UK's tech future during US President Donald Trump's state visit to the UK in September last year.

It was also right in the middle of his attempts to get Trump to lift export bans to China of some of the highest performing AI chips, specifically the H200.

An export ban on a less powerful chip had already been lifted. He was, I suggested to him, one of the few people who could walk into the White House to meet Trump, and a few days later meet President Xi Jinping in Beijing.

He made no secret of his views, nor his assessment that he had persuaded Trump of his case.

"President Trump is very clear. He wants America to win and and President Xi wants China to win, and it's possible for both of them too. And the reason for that is because it's not a zero-sum game. The advance of human society is not a zero-sum game."

He is probably the only person in the world that could have spoken that sentence with the authority that he might have heard personally from both these superpower leaders.

However, his view about "zero-sum game" is not backed by many in national security circles.

Their view is that the race to the most advanced forms of AI is entirely zero sum, and requires the West - and the US in particular - to take critical action to hold back Chinese advancement.

The country that creates the most powerful AI systems, from the most powerful chips, will win, in terms of scientific development, of cracking encryption, economic growth and cyber-weapons.

He made a further argument: Far from being a national security challenge, it was, in fact, better for the US that the world "including China" became dependent on US systems, what they called the "American tech stack", with Nvidia chips at its core.

Huang then went even further than that, saying that President Trump "is very clear-eyed" about the idea that "this computing technology is not a national security concern".

He told me "any military is smart enough to build their military on top of their own indigenous technology, and not rely on an adversary to build their technology, build their military capability".

At that time, which is the same moment now being independently investigated over national security concerns and alleged Chinese espionage, Huang was making clear public arguments to lift export bans, and seemed to have a clear idea of President Trump's views.

More than that, he was also disputing the idea that his technology, in China's hands, was any type of national security concern.

Nvidia is the absolute epicentre of the AI tech boom in the US and of the global race for AI supremacy.

Even if the boom turned to bust, Nvidia is still expected to remain in rude health.

It has actual hard revenues of about $400bn this year. Monday's drop of about 4% of its value reflects new and extraordinary risks at this junction of tech and global politics, but the chipmaker is still worth more than $4 trillion.

A food bank that has seen a drop in donations of about 10% each year since 2023 is hoping government stockpiling advice will not affect the public's generosity.

Someone eats a meal provided by Cambridge City Foodbank "every two minutes" and it claims to have provided more than 260,000 in the past year.

In October, the government launched its "Be Ready" campaign and encouraged households to stock up with enough non-perishable food and water to survive for three days in case of an emergency.

Chief executive Steve Clay says he does not know if this will affect the Christmas appeal - their busiest period - but confesses: "It is a concern."

A government spokesperson said it had "no serious evidence of stockpiling or indeed a supply shortage" with the campaign and it had worked with voluntary organisations and charities to address any concerns.

The food bank team estimates it will provide more than 45,000 meals to people in the city between 13 November and 15 January.

Clay says that with cold weather and pressure on spending, Christmas is "more difficult" than the rest of the year.

"Budgets are tighter, more has to be spent on fuel and energy," he said.

"So people are contacting us all the time for emergency support and we need to make sure that the support is always there and is continuing to be there."

Donations are used to purchase emergency hampers, treats or provide advice and assistance.

While the food bank's doors close on Christmas Day, meals they have provided mean more people can enjoy the festivities.

Every pound donated, up to the first £15,000, would be doubled as part of a match-funding commitment.

Dr Liam Loftus, development director of the food bank, said: "As we head into winter and the cold draws in, thousands of individuals and families will be forced to make the heart-breaking choice between heating or eating.

"This winter, can you take two minutes of your time to support our Winter Appeal?

"You'll be helping restore hope and dignity to people facing hardship and providing one of your neighbours with their next meal at what should be one of the happiest times of year."

The government spokesperson said of the Be Ready campaign: "We've worked hand-in-hand with voluntary organisations and charities, including food banks, to address any concerns and ensure the guidance is as accessible as possible.

"Where households can act, that frees up emergency services to prioritise those most in-need during any emergency."

How close is Donald Trump to Jensen Huang?

The Nvidia boss was one of the few business leaders with direct access to the US president. He had met Trump repeatedly, travelled with him to Britain and, in May, joined him on Air Force One for his trip to China.

Jensen Huang wasn't just another tech billionaire seeking the president's ear. He had become an important voice in one of the biggest arguments inside the administration: how much of America's most advanced technology should be allowed to reach China.

Nvidia makes the chips that power the AI revolution. Washington has restricted exports of its most advanced processors to China since 2022, believing they could help Beijing develop its military and technological capabilities.

But enforcing those restrictions is difficult. Chips can be bought legally by customers in countries such as Singapore and Malaysia and then diverted to China. Chinese companies can also rent access to computing power through data centres outside the country.

Jensen Huang has long argued that the restrictions are counterproductive. They shut Nvidia out of a huge market and encourage Chinese companies to develop their own alternatives. Trump appeared sympathetic to this view, allowing Nvidia to resume sales of certain chips to China last year in return for a share of the revenue, although its most advanced Blackwell chips remain off limits.

But that relationship now looks rather more complicated.

The allegations surrounding Jensen Huang's reported affair with Alice Huang, of no relation but a former executive at Singapore-based company Megaspeed, have raised the possibility that a foreign intelligence operation was targeting not just a powerful businessman, but someone with unusually close access to the American president.

US intelligence reportedly suspects Alice Huang of having links to Chinese intelligence. Beijing has rejected the allegations. Nvidia's board says it has no reason to believe company secrets or national security were compromised. But the affair has opened up a much bigger question: what did the administration in Washington know, and what did it do about it?

That question leads directly to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.

His department was responsible for controlling exports of sensitive American technology. It was also being pressed to act on concerns about Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer suspected of helping divert advanced chips to China.

On Thursday, Megaspeed chief executive, Tan Yong Pong, also known as James Tan, said the company "takes its compliance obligations under US export control laws extremely seriously" and is "committed to working constructively and transparently with the US government". He said the company had co-operated with US Commerce Department inspections.

A highly classified memo was shared with Lutnick about the concerns surrounding Alice Huang and Megaspeed. He resisted taking action against the company, a decision that is now under scrutiny.

Other senior officials wanted a tougher response. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was among those who reportedly questioned why Megaspeed had not been placed on the Commerce Department's blacklist.

There were also questions about why an investigation into the Singapore-based company was stopped after Nvidia intervened. The New York Times reported that Nvidia's general counsel contacted Commerce Department investigators probing suspected chip smuggling by Megaspeed invoking a senior Trump appointee. The department allegedly then froze its investigation and handed the case to the Justice Department.

This apparently highlighted a significant disagreement about the direction of Trump's China policy. Huang wanted access to the Chinese market. Other officials were supposedly worried about the national security consequences. Lutnick was caught in the middle.

Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang summoned to testify before Congress about affair with alleged Chinese spy

The rise and fall of Jensen Huang - how the tech superstar became mired in scandal

Members of Congress from both parties want answers. Democrats have launched an investigation into how the Commerce Department vetted Chinese companies approved to buy AI chips. Republicans are also questioning the administration's approach.

And Jensen Huang's departure has not eased the pressure.

Republican representative John Moolenaar, who chairs the House Select Committee on China, said it was in the national interest for Nvidia and other American AI firms to succeed, but that companies "should never jeopardise our nation's security" by giving Chinese firms access to their most advanced chips.

Senator Elizabeth Warren, the top Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, said Huang's resignation did not absolve him of responsibility, and urged Lutnick to explain why export control loopholes remain open.

Meanwhile Jensen Huang's team told Republican lawmakers on Wednesday that he plans to cooperate with their request to testify behind closed doors.

The White House has not responded to the BBC's request for comment.

It has, however, told the New York Post that Trump has complete confidence in Lutnick, describing him as "the most transformative commerce secretary in modern history".

That is a fairly emphatic show of support, particularly amid reports that officials are weighing whether Lutnick should be forced out.

There are some obvious questions. If Lutnick had indeed been warned about the risks, why did his department fail to act? And if other senior officials were indeed pressing for action, why did it take so long?

The BBC has contacted the Commerce Department for comment. But there is an even bigger question for Trump.

The president cultivated a close relationship with Huang. He was directly involved in decisions about chip sales to China. And, according to reporting in the New York Times, he was briefed on the intelligence concerns.…

Microsoft has said it is "deeply sorry" for the service outage to its products, including Outlook and Teams, which has caused disruption around the world.

Services were broadly recovering by Friday afternoon, nearly 24 hours after issues began. Microsoft said it was making "encouraging progress", but added it does not know when services will fully recover.

The outage hit more than 70 countries, disrupting everything from business operations to government services and personal users. More than 430 million people use the affected products worldwide.

Microsoft said it was a technical issue introduced during a "network capacity upgrade" and not related to cyber or artificial intelligence agents.

Experts said the event was a "stark reminder" of how heavily businesses and vital services rely on a small group of big tech providers.

Users began reporting they were having trouble accessing Microsoft 365 products on Thursday.

By Friday, the far-reaching issue was affecting institutions from the Japanese government and the Philippines Supreme Court to the Australian spy agency, and trains, hospitals and courts in North America.

Why is Microsoft's outage lasting so long and will emails be lost?

Courts, spies and MPs: How the Microsoft outage has been felt around the world

In the UK, some parts of the NHS, including GPs and hospitals, were affected , as were some schools and police forces.

UK cyber minister Liz Lloyd said the incident had "limited" impact on critical frontline services such as 999 calls, and there had been no disruption to the transport network.

In Canada, however, the national rail network said passengers may not be able to receive email updates about their trips, and hospitals across the country also had issues with emails.

In the US, staff members from the House of Representatives told Politico it had set back an entire day of legislative work as everything was on Microsoft's Outlook.

Singapore's government acknowledged some of its systems had been impacted, and in India, the outage disrupted work for many on Friday.

In Turkey, advisers and officials attending the COP31 climate summit in Antalya were left frustrated by being unable to access Outlook.

The issues also affected smaller businesses and individuals.

Peter Pentz, a winemaker in South Africa, said his entire business was basically brought to a "standstill".

His winery's communication with exports was also brought to a standstill, he said, and "critical production work" was been halted as the Cape West Coast winery "relies on these systems for parts of our day-to-day operations".

Georgia from Staffordshire in England said she was due to complete her first house purchase today after waiting eight months to get to this point - but the outage has delayed that.

"The solicitor mentioned there may be a delay due to not being able to contact other agencies.

"We're not the only one completing today, there are hundreds of houses and for them to ring everyone in time is unfeasible," Georgia said.

Microsoft first acknowledged users in the Americas were unable to access Exchange Online mailboxes at 17:54 GMT on Thursday, and shortly after warned the disruption was possibly affecting Microsoft 365 globally.

While it launched an investigation and engineers began working to restore services, by 04:36 on Friday Microsoft was reporting only a "partial recovery" in some parts of the world.

By 13:32, the tech giant said there were "broader improvements" in North America, "sustained improvements" across much of Europe and "encouraging recovery signals" in the Asia Pacific region.

Microsoft said it restored services gradually due to the scale of the problem and to help ensure services remain stable once they are up and running again.

"We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners," a Microsoft spokesperson said.

"We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously."

Microsoft said it has no "ETA" for when services will be fully recovered.

A full post-incident report will be released once Microsoft has completed a review.

Experts said while workers may have been happy to not have email access for the day, the incident showed the dependence many organisations have on these cloud-based services.

"The global Microsoft outage is a stark reminder of how heavily we rely on a handful of big tech providers," said Rob Demain, chief executive of cybersecurity firm e2e-assure.

Matt Saunders, field chief technology officer at tech consultancy Adaptavist, said it would be challenging to mitigate against a similar problem.

"Classic IT disaster planning strategies suggest using a second service for resilience, but in practice, it's almost impossible for a business to function without tools such as Microsoft," he said .

"In the wake of this outage, organisations must have a plan in place for how to work without such tools, for when incidents like this occur."

While Kimi Antonelli was making history as the youngest Formula 1 world champion earlier this month, a British teenager was taking his own steps to a glittering career in the sport.

Freddie Slater made his debut in the free practice sessions at both the Mexican and Sao Paulo Grand Prix.

Slater, who grew up in Stratford-upon-Avon and was educated in Bromsgrove, was handed his first official F1 outing by Audi, and the 18-year-old is one of Britain's brightest motorsport prospects.

He has so far had successful seasons in karting and cars, most recently finishing runner up in the Formula 3 Championship, and told the BBC his latest experiences were "surreal".

"You're doing 350kph (217mph) into turn one at Mexico, I've never done anything like it, honestly it's just incredible," he said.

"(In) 2023, I was still in karting, then last year I was in the Formula Regional Championship which I won, and this year Formula 3."

Formula 3 is a support series organised by the FIA and competes alongside Formula 1, visiting the same tracks and racing on the same weekends.

It's an opportunity for drivers to get themselves noticed and for Slater it allowed him to become the first driver to be signed to Audi's driver development programme.

That has led to the recent outings in the team's Formula 1 cars.

"It's been great to have the support of Audi and the support of people like team principal Mattia Binotto and racing director Allan McNish.

"I didn't expect this opportunity to come so early if I'm honest. I just love speed and sitting in that F1 car was just the most surreal and incredible feeling. I've waited my whole life for this.

"I think the big difference with the F1 paddock is the amount of people, you have hundreds of people behind you, to get that car on track."

Slater's time in the car was cut short on both occasions due to mechanical problems - not uncommon for teams in practice sessions because both the driver and teams are learning the track and what setup works best. He adds that the opportunity itself to drive an F1 car was a dream come true.

"Honestly, I couldn't believe it when I was told I was getting to drive... it was just incredible getting those laps behind me with the forces and speeds involved".

Racing from a young age meant balancing exams and coursework with travelling around the world.

Slater's former headmaster, Mike Marie at Bromsgrove Preparatory School, said: "We're so proud of Freddie after having his first practice at an F1 weekend. My memories of Freddie were of him coming into school in year four with trophies bigger than he was, always incredibly talented, we wish him the best of luck on the world stage."

Slater recalls his time at school and the support he received there fondly: "I had to take prolonged absences to go racing, but also the friendships I've built up, the effort I put in at a young age."

Slater's family still live in Warwickshire and he is the oldest of five children.

"I love coming home after a busy race weekend, it's nice to unwind away from the pressure of the paddock, but also to catch up with family and friends.

"Motorsport is in my family, my dad used to race himself, my two brothers are also climbing the ladder, the youngest of which is 10 and just started karting."

Slater will now be gearing up for a season in Formula 2 with Invicta Racing, the current championship leaders. It means he will be around the paddock more often on a grand prix weekend - an opportunity he is relishing.

"Getting to Formula 1 is super difficult because the margins are so small and the drivers are at the top of their game.

"Of course I want to win a championship, that's got to be the goal every year, but it's also to develop as a driver.

"It's a tough sport in terms of how long the years are, there is so much testing, and training, that's the side people don't see."

Slater is not due on-track again until next year, however he will still be putting in the hours on the simulator and hitting the gym on a daily basis to stay fit.

With the support of Audi, he is also likely to feature in another practice session in the not-too-distant future.

Hundreds of billions of dollars have been wiped off the value of Nvidia after the US chipmaker announced an independent investigation would be carried out into its chief executive's affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

The tech firm saw its shares fall by about 4% by close of trade on Monday after Jensen Huang admitted having an extramarital affair.

Nvidia's probe came after reports that the US believed the Nvidia boss had been targeted in an espionage campaign by China.

However, China has rejected the claims, with its foreign ministry saying allegations about Chinese spies were "entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China".

Nvidia said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised, but a statement by the firm's board of directors said it would begin an investigation in "light of recent reporting that founder and chief executive Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort".

US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report , external .

The report said Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington last spring warning that the Nvidia boss was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.

Alice Huang was managing director of Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has had dealings with Nvidia.

Jensen Huang admitted he was "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children. He added he was "committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security" and would cooperate with the investigation.

The Nvidia co-founder has also been requested to appear for a joint closed-door briefing for several Congressional committees next week.

Members of the US House Foreign Affairs Committee last week asked Jensen Huang to appear for a closed-door briefing on his interactions with Alice Huang, as well as Nvidia's security protocols around espionage.

"Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC's [China's] access to sensitive US technology and information," congressmen Brian Mast, John Moolenaar, and Rick Crawford wrote in a letter.

"It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which US national security has been placed at risk."

After Nvidia's investigation was announced, other big tech bosses, including Elon Musk, came out in support of Jensen Huang to continue leading the firm.

US President Donald Trump said the Nvidia boss was an "honourable guy".

However, the news sparked a sell-off in Nvidia's shares, with about $250bn (£190bn) wiped of the company's market value.

While Nvidia shares fell, the US stock market opened the week on a positive note after last week's turmoil, with Nvidia's rival chipmakers benefiting.

But analysts suggested the hit to the company would be short-lived. Victoria Fernandez, chief market strategist at Crossmark Global Investments said investors would not abandon Nvidia, because the chipmaker was so important to the AI industry.

"Nvidia is the core of this AI trade, and without them, all these other pieces start to fall apart because the financing's not there," she told the BBC.

Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia, which is central to making the hardware for emerging AI technologies, with two other engineers in 1993.

Its chips were initially designed for gaming, but he decided to turn its focus on AI development, turning it into the world's second most valuable company.

A key concern for investors going forward is what would happen to Nvidia if Jensen Huang was removed from the company, as Fernandez said there was "no natural successor" to the chief executive.

Jensen Huang, unlike other founders in the tech industry, is vulnerable to any move by Nvidia's board of directors to oust him.

He owns only around 3.5% of the company, and Nvidia operates on a single class voting structure, meaning his stake would not be enough to act as a veto power over any board decision.

By contrast, many tech founders who lead their companies, including Mark Zuckerberg of Meta and Musk of Tesla and SpaceX, hold significant percentages of multiple types of stock in their companies.

Fernandez said she does not believe the board will remove Jensen Huang as chief executive, unless there is glaring evidence of wrongdoing related to national security or intellectual property, "but I bet they start bringing someone up as his number two, to have there for the future."

The modest fall in its shares mean investors believe it is unlikely he will step down or be removed as chief executive, but that the outcome of the investigation will be closely watched.

Even people who do not directly own shares in Nvidia can be affected by rises and falls in its value. Pensions or savings invested in pots which have stakes in the company through index tracking funds can be impacted, for example.

What we know so far about Jensen Huang's affair with suspected Chinese spy

Nvidia chips have been a major focus of the AI race between the US and China and the White House has previously imposed controls on where its advanced products can be sold.

The H200, Nvidia's second most advanced semiconductor, had previously been restricted by Washington over concerns that it would give China's technology industry an edge over the US.

But Jensen Huang has been against restricting the sale of Nvidia's chips to China, arguing that it would be better for the global rollout of AI to be powered by US technology.

In January, the Trump administration said it would allow the company to sell its H200 chips to Chinese customers under certain conditions.

Additional reporter by Samira Hussain, North America business correspondent.

Recent university graduate Lotte Underwood is a public relations executive with a twist - she spends more time using AI than actually doing PR.

Underwood, 25, joined London-based PR agency Fight or Flight in November last year, in the new role of "AI associate" after completing a degree and then a masters in marketing.

She's part of a recently established, dedicated AI team that has built around 30 AI agents. Specific tasks include industry research, client reporting, media interview preparation, helping clients create clearer briefs, and image generation.

A big part of Underwood's job is to manage those agents, check their outputs and feed those to the team members who are dealing directly with clients and the media.

Another key responsibility of hers is to monitor how clients appear in the responses from AI tools like ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and others.

"A huge part is being in client meetings and calls to work out what is actually going to be most helpful from these agents," says Underwood.

AI is seen as one of the main factors behind graduate job cuts , but companies are also creating dedicated AI-specific graduate roles like Underwood's.

Dillan Patel, for example, joined engineering software company Stride 18 months ago as an intern. A business management graduate, he was put to work developing an internal chatbot designed to capture the knowledge of a senior staff member transitioning into retirement.

Patel, 24, is now an AI automation analyst, tasked with developing further internal agents to provide specific information to individual teams, while also identifying which manual or repetitive tasks across the company could be done by AI.

"My role focuses on finding practical ways to use technology, automation, data and AI to improve how we operate," says Coventry-based Patel.

Such AI savvy graduates are also in demand from companies like ArvatoConnect, an outsourced contact centre company.

CEO Debra Maxwell says the company's usual graduate intake is on hold this year, but she plans to resume it next year with a bigger focus on AI.

"We would be looking for more AI-disruptor type roles, where you can challenge us as an organisation to think more holistically about where AI can be applied and where we could grow our business from," says London-based Maxwell.

"We see our graduates as not filling administrative roles, but actually adding value to the organisation in a different way."

Maxwell adds: "For example, one of our recent graduates is using AI to do deep dives on specific markets, and provide more information for when we're bidding [for new contracts]. It's basically giving him a more rounded role."

If AI can make a graduate job bigger and more integral to the organisation, Maxwell argues that companies can create a more loyal, engaged workforce that is able to contribute more meaningfully, much earlier.

Research from consultancy PwC found that some graduate roles are assuming more responsibilities because of AI, as it allows companies to demand more senior abilities from junior hires.

For the consultancy's 2026 AI Jobs Barometer , external , it analysed 2.4 million entry-level jobs in the US. It found that the entry-level roles most influenced by AI are now seven times more likely to require traditionally senior-level skills. These include motivational leadership, strategic decision making and team building.

Those entry-level roles with higher expectations have in fact grown 35% since 2019, PwC found, while other entry-level roles actually shrank by 10%.

Cian Clinton, who joined consultancy Valliance last September after graduating from a Bachelor of Science in 2024, says the incorporation of AI into his role makes him feel less like a graduate, and more like an equal team member. He uses around 10 AI agents daily for different tasks.

"Your ideas and your creativity are a lot more valued because you actually get to implement those firsthand, and the responsibility you take on is a lot greater because of that," says London-based Clinton, 23.

"I am now taking on responsibilities which would usually take me four or five years to get to."

His career progression, he believes, will now be faster as a result.

"AI is killing the 'pyramid' approach…progression is no longer based on your knowledge bank. Now it's more based on your critical thinking and understanding of the processes," says Clinton.

There's no doubt Underwood, Patel and Clinton are developing valuable AI knowledge which can help them across their careers.

But with their time at work so focused on AI, does it matter how much - or how little - time they're spending learning about the professional field they're supposed to be operating in?

Underwood says she'd like to still pick up the traditional PR skills her role isn't currently focused on, but is confident of her future in the agency's growing AI team.

"There's certain things that I haven't had the chance to do yet, like directly pitching to the media. I absolutely plan to do this," she says.

Graduates becoming too AI-centric is an issue for Simon Pratt, chief operating officer at Portman Finance Group. He says being able to use AI effectively is important, but the company's two-year graduate programme is fully centred on "learning the trade".

"Our graduates rotate across four areas at six-month intervals, working directly alongside senior relationship managers to learn their trade," Northampton-based Pratt explains.

"They'll learn all of our financial products, how to draft credit papers for submission to lenders, and how to build meaningful relationships with our customers. They'll progress to running transactions from start to finish."

Claire Reed, PwC UK's chief technology and innovation officer, believes graduate roles that are too AI heavy won't necessarily provide graduates long-term career progression.

"There will be no graduate job now that doesn't require a baseline of AI literacy," says Glasgow-based Reed.…
