Pochettino to take charge of two final USMNT matches

He has signed two-and-a-half-year United contract

Mauricio Pochettino’s switch from the US men’s national team to Manchester United has been confirmed. Pochettino will guide the US through a pair of Concacaf Nations League matches on Saturday and Tuesday before joining United, for whom his first game will come at Liverpool next Sunday.

The former Chelsea, Tottenham and Southampton manager has signed a two-and-a-half-year deal to replace Michael Carrick, who was sacked on Thursday after leading United to their worst start to a season in four decades. United have won one of their past 11 games and are in the Premier League’s relegation zone.

United made Pochettino their first-choice target after it became clear Carrick would be dismissed. They only held talks with the Argentinian, despite interest in the former Newcastle manager Eddie Howe and Julian Nagelsmann. United’s leadership group selected Pochettino over other candidates and had the decision to appoint him signed off by Sir Jim Ratcliffe this week.

The club were attracted to Pochettino based on his personality, hoping he can turn things around at United by building a strong culture within the dressing room. United sought a more experienced coach after Carrick, feeling Pochettino’s long-term record of player development and clear philosophy would suit the needs of United at the moment.

Pochettino signed a new four-year contract with US Soccer in August, an expansive deal that offered the Argentinian greater control over youth development and the overall direction of the men’s programme. To secure his services, United have paid the US federation about $10m (£7.5m), with an additional fee paid to secure the services of Pochettino’s longtime assistants.

United’s players not on international duty were told on Thursday they did not need to return to training until next week. With the second of the US’s two games against Haiti finishing in the early hours of Wednesday GMT, Pochettino’s first day with United is expected to be Thursday.

“The opportunity to represent the USA crest was one of the greatest honours of my career. We are so grateful to the players for their commitment, to the fans for their belief, and to the federation for always supporting our staff and creating the opportunities to impact the culture of soccer in this great country,” Pochettino said on Friday.

“We want to thank Cindy Parlow Cone, JT Batson and Dan Helfrich for their partnership and incredible working relationships throughout our time here. There is tremendous talent in the US player pool from the youth teams through to the senior team, and it’s one of the reasons we have so much belief for the future of US Soccer. You will always have a special place in our hearts, and we will be supporting the teams whenever they step on the field.”

Pochettino was hired by US Soccer in September 2024, brought on to steer the US through their first home World Cup in 32 years. Over the ensuing two years he compiled a 21-12-2 record and guided the team to the World Cup last 16, results that stack up favourably alongside other US coaches.

He earned praise in the US for his enthusiasm and for putting together the US men’s greatest group stage at a World Cup, a performance that included a 4-1 dismantling of Paraguay that will go down as the team’s best 90-minute performance at the tournament. All of that early progress, though, was wiped out by a 4-1 loss to Belgium in the last 16, a result marred by the federation’s – and Pochettino’s – handling of the red card controversy surrounding US forward Folarin Balogun.

It was not his only lowlight: there was the shocking fourth-place finish in the 2024-25 Nations League and a bitterly disappointing loss to Mexico in the 2025 Gold Cup final. The US were thrashed by top-level competition in friendly matches, and Pochettino sometimes struggled to connect with players, primarily the Milan midfielder Christian Pulisic. Others, such as Juventus midfielder Weston McKennie, found themselves in and out of the picture on a regular basis.

Pochettino leaves the US with a glimmer of hope for the future. Across his tenure, 75 players earned at least one cap for the US. In the months after signing his extension, he did well to integrate more than a dozen newcomers into the squad during a four-match international window during which the US went undefeated across four matches.

Steve Cherundolo, head coach of the US U-23 national team, will lead the senior team’s December camp, which will feature a roster of primarily Major League Soccer players.

United’s captain, Bruno Fernandes, has rejected a second offer of a new contract but the club are confident of getting the midfielder to commit his future. The 32-year-old’s deal runs until the end of the season but United have the option to trigger a further year.

Fernandes would be allowed to speak to clubs abroad in January if United have not activated that clause. He has previously had interest from Saudi Arabia and Galastasaray.

Fernandes won the Professional Footballers’ Association’s men’s player of the year award last season after helping United to third in the league with a record-breaking 21 assists but his form has dipped. He took aim at Carrick’s tactics after last month’s defeat by Como in the Champions League.

Coach was ‘transparent’ in dealings with club, federation

Pochettino had signed deal to stay with US through 2030

There were always going to be tears at Mauricio Pochettino’s news conference at US Soccer’s national training center on Friday. It was only a matter of when. Pochettino is famously emotional, and nobody in attendance had to wait long for the waterworks – they came during his introductory remarks, as he thanked the US Soccer executives flanking him for the opportunity to guide the US men. He grew emotional again as he addressed his impending departure for Manchester United, one announced just hours earlier.

“I think [the decision was],” Pochettino said, pausing to compose himself, “one of the most difficult decisions of our careers. Thank you guys. Thank you so much.”

The news conference read very much as a farewell to Pochettino, but there is still work to be done. The Argentinian will guide the USMNT through a pair of Concacaf Nations League quarter-final matches against Haiti on Saturday and Tuesday. In the meantime, the future United coach did his best to address questions about his departure and what comes next.

“These moments are not easy decisions,” a reflective Pochettino told the media. “Normally it’s the opposite. Normally you get sacked and you cry because you want to stay and you’re sacked by [the club]. It’s a tough decision but at the same time we are excited for the next step forward.”

Pochettino characterized United’s interest and negotiations as having come together at the last minute, essentially, with contact between the two sides first made Sunday.

“We cannot underestimate the staff and the players. When things became big and big and big, the players are very sensitive and the staff are too – they start to feel things as well. [Everything] was so quick, because we arrived here last Friday and Sunday afternoon this situation started to appear and some contact. We were very transparent, we were talking with [US Soccer CEO] JT [Batson] and the federation.”

Details were quickly ironed out between the sides, with the club and federation agreeing Pochettino would remain with the US through the upcoming matches.

“[Thursday], when things were positive in the way the agreement was, we had a meeting and I communicated to the players and the whole staff. I want to say thank you because they were very supportive and they really understand the situation and they know us – how committed we are for the next two games. The decision between the federation and Manchester United , to agree that we’ll continue with our job in the camp; [nothing] can change our commitment and how important the next two games are.”

Pochettino and the US federation touted his contract renewal in August as the start of something new and significant, with the coach given a larger role in the overall direction of the US men at every level. That went by the wayside when United came knocking.

“They know that there are not too many opportunities that can happen in your career like [this one with Manchester United],” Pochettino said. “When they arrive, it’s difficult to turn down. But I want to make it clear, when we decided together to [stay another four years], it was always the commitment for the federation, too. Maybe the four games [in the September/October window] if we lose them, maybe you start to put pressure [on me]. And maybe something can be in a different way.

“Or even in the future,” he continued, “Things can happen. The federation and maybe new people arrive or don’t, or maybe have different ideas and you say, ‘We are thinking in different directions’ and maybe they say ‘Mauricio, maybe you need to go home.’ We cannot think in these extremes – I think we were very committed and never thought this would happen so quickly.”

African philosophies including exploring how lessons from the past can shape the present and near future have inspired a film festival coming to Manchester .

The festival is part of See My World’s year-round programme showcasing pan-African arts, culture and events.

It reflects the determination among creatives and activists in Manchester to build on the legacy of the 1945 Pan-African Congress in Manchester – which connected luminaries of postwar independence movements with a shared vision of liberation – after last year’s 80th anniversary commemorations .

See My World’s CEO and artistic director, Tunde Adekoya, said this month’s film festival was taking inspiration from across the spectrum of pan-African thought, including the works of Kenyan writers John Mbiti, an Anglican theologian who died in 2019, and Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o, the author of the groundbreaking 1986 book Decolonising the Mind who died last year.

Both writers rejected the colonial conceit that African thought was inferior, stressed the importance of community and saw reclaiming African ways of knowing as essential to a people’s self-understanding.

While Mbiti sought common ground between African religions and Christianity, Ngũgĩ was a Marxist. He argued colonialism was motivated by cultural and economic conquest, and that European powers used language as their sharpest instrument. Ngũgĩ famously abandoned English to write in Gikuyu, a Bantu language mainly spoken in Kenya and criticised the role missionary Christianity played in colonial rule.

Adekoya said: “It’s a day dedicated to pan-African and global majority films from the north of England with exclusive premieres of documentaries we’ve been working on, which weave together expressions of liberation through art forms like poetry and dance.

“The whole idea is that it’s like a playground in search of strategies of liberation, using the festival as a way to explore different philosophies.

“John Mbiti explores the philosophy and spiritual understandings of time through the concept of Sasa na Zamani – in which the past informs everything that happens moving forward. That reflects how we constantly go back to pan-African histories to inform how we progress.”

Film-makers have been invited to submit films lasting up to 30 minutes from across genres, with no screening fees charged.

As well as submissions, the festival will feature documentaries produced by See My World. They include Homage, a “cinematic love letter to dance” that traces a culture through present-day portraits illustrating dance artists and archival material from Manchester, telling a story of joy, loss, migration, rhythm and resistance. Adekoya added: “The idea is that we would go against the norm of how film festivals are, because when we think about decolonisation, we think about how structures have been created to alienate and exclude communities.

“It’s very important to restore the dignity of these people, which was taken from them in life and in death,” said Carolina Dias dos Reis, a government official who travelled to Boston to sign the agreement with Harvard.

The existence of the skulls was revealed in 2022 , and Brazilian researchers sought their repatriation from Harvard, but said they faced a drawn-out process that only moved forward after the Brazilian government became involved in late 2024.

In recent months, concerns grew that Donald Trump’s sometimes hostile behaviour towards his Brazilian counterpart, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, could derail the repatriation. But everything worked out.

“We need to recover our past as a country, however difficult and violent it was, so that we can understand what we are living through in the present: the consequences and scars of structural racism,” added Reis.

Slavery was abolished in 1888, but nearly a century and a half later, Afro-Brazilians make up the majority of the population while occupying the bottom of every socioeconomic indicator, dominating the statistics on hunger , poverty , gender-based violence and victims of homicides committed by criminals or the police .

During the repatriation ceremony in Rio de Janeiro, Ivanir dos Santos, a history professor and a cleric of the Afro-Brazilian religion Candomblé, poured a glass of water on to the ground as researchers received the suitcase.

“It was a ritual act because you cannot deal with the remains of our ancestors without paying reverence to them. This is not a research object … for us, that person is still alive in memory and as our ancestor,” he said.

It is not precisely known who the skulls belonged to. The one taken to Salvador is believed to have belonged to a man who took part in the most significant urban slave revolt in Brazilian history, in 1835, when about 600 African Muslims attempted to seize control of what was then the country’s second most important city. They were ultimately defeated by police, who killed 70 rebels.

The man died at a hospital, and a US diplomat, Gideon T Snow, is believed to have sent the skull to Boston.

The Bahia Islamic Cultural Centre, one of the most active campaigners for its repatriation, has named the man Arakunrin, meaning brother in Yoruba.

Even less is known about the other person: initially, only that they were “an individual … exhumed from the ‘streets of Rio de Janeiro’” in the 1860s. Brazilian government officials, however, said on Wednesday that Harvard researchers had told them that some features – including that the skull was smaller than that of an adult man but larger than that of a child – suggested it may have belonged to a woman.

Bruno Veras, a historian who was part of the group that closely followed the repatriation, cross-referenced diaries, letters and maps of the city and believes the skull may have been taken from a cemetery for newly arrived Africans who either did not survive the long Atlantic crossing or died soon after disembarking .

The person believed to have taken it to the US was Walter Hunnewell, a student from a wealthy Boston family. He was part of an expedition led by the Harvard professor Louis Agassiz, who was in Brazil trying to document physical types to support his racist theories.

“To steal a skull and take it to another country was violent even in the context of racist research,” said Veras.

Researchers in forensic anthropology will now try to confirm the sex of the individuals and other information through measurements of the skulls – the one in Salvador is complete, while the one in Rio is missing its jaw – and microscopic analyses. If necessary, they will seek authorisation to carry out genetic or dating tests.

“This history of slavery cannot be undone,” said Irina Feisthauer Silveira, a diplomat who carried one of the skulls. “But acknowledging the mistakes of the past with transparency is a first step towards building a more equal, just and less violent future.”

Exclusive: investigation finds prescriptions for children under 12, as experts stress need for specialist supervision and long-term monitoring

Hundreds of children in England are receiving prescriptions for GLP-1 medications, including some younger than 12, the Guardian can reveal.

GLP-1 medications were initially developed to help people with type 2 diabetes control their blood sugar levels, but have since become a popular slimming aid, with products such as Wegovy and Mounjaro becoming household names.

While social media is awash with adults who have lost weight with GLP-1s, data shows a number of children are also being prescribed them.

A Guardian investigation has revealed that in the financial year 2025-26 there were 419 prescriptions issued to children under the age of 18, 10 of which were for children under the age of 12.

And in the four months from April to July this year, 341 prescriptions for GLP-1s were issued to children, 15 of whom were under the age of 12.

The figures, obtained from the NHS Business Services Authority through freedom of information requests, relate to prescriptions in England and dispensed in a community setting anywhere in the UK.

However, they do not cover those prescribed and dispensed via private prescriptions, in prisons, and in hospitals, meaning the figures are likely to be a considerable underestimate.

One private clinic for children has previously revealed it has more than 200 patients receiving the jabs. It is also unclear whether the GLP-1 figures reflect medications that are being given primarily for weight loss.

Martin Whyte, a professor of metabolic medicine at the University of Surrey, said the number of prescriptions was still small relative to the scale of childhood obesity, but those taking the drugs needed long-term change to their lifestyles.

He said: “The important thing is that children who start them do so within specialist services, with support for diet, growth and wellbeing, and a plan for the long term.

“That includes regular monitoring of growth and puberty, nutritional intake, mental health and eating behaviours, and side effects. This matters partly because we know weight tends to return when the drugs are stopped, and partly because we still have limited data on use over many years in growing young people.”

The rising use of GLP-1s comes as levels of childhood obesity are increasing. Figures from the National Child Measurement Programme show that 10.7% of reception-year children (ages 4 and 5) are obese, while that rises to 22.8% for children in year 6 (ages 10 and 11).

According to the World Health Organization (WHO), 400 million children and adolescents aged between five and 19 were overweight in 2024, including 170 million living with obesity.

As part of efforts for early intervention, the NHS began piloting Complications from Excess Weight (CEW) clinics from 2021, aimed at children aged two to 16 with severe obesity.

In May, NHS England revealed almost 6,500 children have since been referred to such clinics , including more than 400 younger than four.

Hundreds of young people have received weight-loss medications through such services – although only some CEW clinics can access funding to offer GLP-1s, and these are typically dispensed through hospital pharmacies.

Dr Dunia Ismail, a consultant paediatrician who runs a CEW clinic, said experts were now looking at widening the use of GLP-1s in such settings. “We have been sticking to 12 [years], although now we are looking at expanding that to eight-plus once licence-approved,” she said.

Last month, new global guidelines from the WHO stated obesity medications, including GLP-1s, should not be given to children under the age of 10.

However, recent data from a trial involving 165 children aged 6 to under 12 – run by the pharmaceutical company Novo Nordisk, which produces Wegovy and Victoza – has suggested GLP-1s can help young children with obesity.

Julian Hamilton-Shield, a professor in diabetes and metabolic endocrinology and a clinician at the Bristol Complications CEW clinic, said typically children who receive semaglutide at CEW clinics had been unable to lose weight through standard dietary and nutritional advice and psychological support.

“Probably, in the vast majority of cases, they have a secondary comorbidity such as type 2 diabetes, obstructive sleep apnoea, liver disease, intracranial hypertension – you name it, they’ve got it,” he said. “So it’s been used as an adjunct after standard therapies haven’t really helped. However, it is used quite frequently and it is a very effective drug.”

Hamilton-Shield stressed GLP-1 medications were given to children who have very high excess weight. “You’d call it morbid obesity if you were classifying it as adults,” he said.

The use of GLP-1s in children has reignited a debate about the drivers of childhood obesity, but experts say it is important to avoid blaming patients or their families.

“We’re a health service that delivers health to the people who require it. We’re not one that makes moral judgments about people,” said Hamilton-Shield. “Nobody’s saying that every child who’s a bit heavy should have a GLP-1.”

Hamilton-Shield added: “These children and young people are from very complex backgrounds, have enormous lack of self-esteem. They’re not attending school. They’ve got all these complications. They’ve got all the stigma. And when you actually give them a drug that helps them to lose maybe 25, 30kg, [it is] the first time they feel they have any agency in their lives at all, and that will have a transformative effect in its own right.”

Ismail also stressed the importance of GLP-1s for children. “We know now that obesity is not a choice, it’s a condition,” she said. “We’re giving them GLP-1s because there is nothing else you can do at this stage. Otherwise, they will die young, they will have heart disease, they will have diabetes … It’s just terrible what could happen to them if we don’t.”

Exclusive: Report says restricting cars and freeing up pavement space could be a cheap way to entice shoppers

The long decline of the high street is a problem that has gripped British governments for years. But what if there was a solution no one had considered before – doing it all on the cheap?

Spending less money is, admittedly, just one element of a report led by the urban thinktank Create Streets. But it does argue that rather than multimillion-pound revamps, a better answer could be smaller changes aimed at making town and city centres more appealing.

Central to this, the study says, is trying to banish, or at least tame, motor traffic, because too often urban centres are places “designed to be driven through, not for time to be spent in”.

As well as citing a lack of imagination, the report blames planning regulations that favour conformity and clutter and too often treat speeding cars as a given, to which everything else must adjust.

“The default high street is engineered for traffic and furnished from a catalogue: a tarmac pavement, guardrails penning people at the kerb, litter bins ordered from a procurement catalogue, a row of plastic planters – public investment that is joyless,” it says.

While planners have traditionally focused on car access as a metric for thriving town centres, calculations for the Create Streets report suggest that replacing parking with other kerbside infrastructure, including bike spaces or outside drinking and dining areas, creates more economic value.

It found that one parking space in the high street of a market town is typically used by about 3.5 vehicles a day, bringing in just over £73,000 a year in spending to nearby shops.

But the same 12 square metres, if used to hold nine share e-bikes, generates an average of 13 trips a day, with over £146,000 a year in spending, even taking into account the lower average spend per person.

In a busier city, where share bikes would be used more frequently, the estimated total annual spend rises to more than £300,000.

Repurposing the space for outside dining brings less dramatic gains, but in a city centre it can still amount to about £120,000 in extra annual spending.

The report, also produced by Cyclehoop, which makes bike storage, calls for a cultural rethink involving low-cost tweaks that rip away ugly and unnecessary street furniture and make better use of kerbsides.

Calling use by families “the indicator species of a healthy high street”, the report cites what is known as “the wrist test” – whether it feels safe to let go of a young child’s wrist so they can roam with some freedom.

This is best done, it argues, by removing the threat of speeding motor vehicles and not by trying to mitigate their impact. It calls the removal of pedestrian guardrails next to roads “the most cost-effective upgrade for the majority of high streets”, saying they are an eyesore with minimal safety benefits.

The report says “the absurdity of modern public realm management” is exemplified by Secured by Design, policy guidelines on cutting neighbourhood crime. These can, critics point out, mean benches and plants are removed on the advice of police, supposedly to discourage antisocial behaviour.

Andy Burnham, the prime minister, has pledged to try to reverse the decline of high streets, announcing in September a £210m regeneration fund.

However, the bulk of the money will go into buildings: turning old shops into shared workspaces or community cafes, or keeping pubs and clubs in business.

The report argues that renovating buildings is pointless if the street outside is unappealing. To reduce clutter, it says, there should be “a presumption of removal where an item cannot be justified”.

The effects can be dramatic, the report says, pointing to examples including Altrincham in Cheshire, where the creation of a walkable, car-free urban area helped see retail vacancies fall from over 30% to 7% in less than a decade.

Such initiatives do not have to be expensive, it claims, noting the example of an unused patch of land next to a church in Grimsby which was turned into a park for less than £20,000.

“Streets that are ugly are not so because councils lack the desire to change them, but because the system is counting the maintenance liabilities, not the benefits,” said David Milner of Create Streets.

“What works is cheap: trees in the ground, benches people want to sit on, clutter taken away.

“So much of what is built now seems to be temporary, looking more like road works than public realm improvements, so we encourage the concept of permanence; more trees in the ground, not in giant plant pots, for example.”

A spokesperson for the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government said: “We support local leaders to make decisions on pedestrianisation based on their communities’ needs.

“Our Hope on the High Street strategy will help local people revive town centres by protecting community assets, bringing derelict buildings back into use and tackling the spread of vape and gambling shops.

“Funding is available for local leaders to spend on their priorities, including pedestrianising and regenerating their high streets if they so wish.”

Hannah Walker says systems designed to minimise expenditure in the name of efficiency can end up less capable of fulfilling their actual purpose

The article by Steven Strogatz and Alex Townsend on the dangers of excessive optimisation identifies a problem extending far beyond mathematics and artificial intelligence ( The efficiency trap: why optimising everything can backfire, badly, 8 November ).

The widespread adoption of just-in-time supply chains illustrates it perfectly. By eliminating inventories and spare capacity, businesses reduced costs and improved efficiency, but frequently transferred those savings into risks that remained invisible until something went wrong. The disruption of global manufacturing during the pandemic exposed the consequences.

The same thinking has shaped public services and national defence. Hospital beds, experienced staff, strategic stockpiles and redundant infrastructure can all appear wasteful when measured against immediate demand. Yet their value lies precisely in their availability when circumstances cease to be normal.

Europe’s dependence on American military capabilities provides a particularly troubling example. What appeared financially efficient in peacetime has created strategic vulnerabilities as the reliability of US commitments comes into question.

The fundamental error is not optimisation itself, but optimising the wrong objective. A system designed to minimise expenditure may succeed brilliantly at doing so while becoming progressively less capable of fulfilling its actual purpose. Resilience is not inefficiency. It is a form of insurance. Like all insurance, the value only becomes apparent when it is needed – usually in a crisis. Hannah Walker Wymondham, Leicestershire

Due to her age and disability, lawyers at Refugee and Migrant Justice applied to the Home Office for her to be granted indefinite leave to remain now rather than having to wait two more decades before becoming eligible. There is a provision to fast-track indefinite leave to remain applications in exceptional circumstances.

However, the Home Office rejected this application, telling her in the first part of the letter that she could return to Nigeria because there are services there for blind people. But the refusal letter concluded: “Your circumstances are not so severe or lacking in potential treatment in India that it would warrant indefinite leave to remain in this case.”

One person on the Home Office data disclosure is a woman from Pakistan aged 103, who will not be eligible for settlement until she is 123 years old.

“In 2022, I got my permission to stay here based on long residence in the UK,” said Comfort. “I’m very disheartened that I may now need to wait nearly 20 years to get indefinite leave to remain.

“I have been living in this country for 26 years. I have found my home here and settled well. I have my friends, my church and do voluntary work. Nick Beales, head of campaigning at Migrant and Refugee Justice, who is supporting Comfort, said: “This woman is blind, in her late 60s and has lived in the UK for a quarter of a century. She meets the rules to remain here and there is no public interest in making her continue to renew her visa.

“Rather than viewing these vulnerable people as human beings, the government is fixated on appearing tough. Shabana Mahmood’s plans to double settlement routes will clearly make these problems even worse, especially as her decision-makers cannot even differentiate between India and Nigeria.

“Government data shows that people over 80 are applying to enter these settlement routes. While it’s unlikely many of these people would survive a 10-year period, Mahmood has not explained what she hopes to achieve by making these octogenarians and older wait two decades before having settlement. The government should admit that their earned settlement model is cruel and counter-productive and scrap these plans once and for all.”

Home Office sources said that corrective action was being taken to re-issue an updated letter to the woman.

A Home Office spokesperson said: “We do not routinely comment on individual cases. All applications for permission to stay in the UK are carefully considered on their individual merits, in line with the immigration rules and based on the information and evidence provided by the applicant.”

One company is proposing elongating the life of the dump, pungent smell and all, several more decades

A s a visual representation of how New York is running out of places to put its waste, the largest active landfill in the state is a striking one. The hulking Seneca Meadows landfill is already the height of the Statue of Liberty and its operators are seeking to raise it even further, to the consternation of nearby residents.

The landfill, situated in the scenic Finger Lakes region in the northern reaches of New York state, has grown since the 1980s to now sprawl across 350 acres of deposited trash, mounded up to the height of around 300ft – roughly the same height of the Statue of Liberty.

“All around the lakes is pretty flat until you see this monster of a hill,” said Mark Pitifer, a marketing administrator at Waterloo Containers, a glass packaging company that sits next to the landfill and is dwarfed by its neighbor. “I mean it’s incredible, it’s like being in downtown New York City only instead of a building, it’s trash.”

Locals in the nearby towns of Waterloo and Seneca Falls, the latter famed as the birthplace of the women’s rights movement in the US, had hoped the bulging landfill would be closed when its permit expired last year. But the operator, Texas-based Waste Connections, has proposed elongating the life of the landfill for several more decades via 47 acres of newly lined disposal cells and adding another 70ft to the trash heap’s height.

As New York state authorities mull whether to grant this expansion, the landfill has become a central point of grievance over the pungent smell, water pollution and planet-heating pollution given off by the places we dump our rubbish. Seneca Meadows is now the largest source of methane, a potent greenhouse gas, in the state, according to a study last year based on researchers using aircraft measurements.

The operator, Waste Connections, did not respond to questions from the Guardian; it defends its environmental protections measures and record in statements on its website.

The increasing size of landfills also raises uncomfortable questions about how much waste we produce and what to do with it. Seneca Meadows receives around 6,000 tons of trash each day from across New York, with 1,500 of those tons originating from New York City, which sends its rubbish to landfills hundreds of miles away that are rapidly filling up and are set to be completely full within the next 16 to 25 years .

If burning rubbish or casually dumping it into rivers and the ocean is too environmentally harmful, what is to be done with our waste beyond continually supersizing landfills to the point they become a major climate , as well as local, hazard?

“We are at the precipice of a crisis,” said Emily Gallagher, a Democratic member of the New York state assembly who recently took a tour of the Seneca Meadows site and has convened a hearing on the state’s waste storage policies.

“There is this huge mountain of trash that is off gassing almost 24 hours a day … contaminating the Finger Lakes, contaminating the groundwater,” she said of the site. “People we met in town are in really bad shape, we need to shut this expansion attempt down now.”

Gallagher said intense lobbying and donations from interests aligned with the plastics and fossil fuels industries has stymied strict measures to reduce waste and enforce more recycling – she estimated 80% of the Seneca Meadows contents could be recycled. But she added there needed to be a broader societal reckoning with the tsunami of trash, much of it from cheap and disposal items, we create.

“We say throwing away but there is no away,” said Gallagher, whose district includes a part of New York City’s borough of Brooklyn. “The problem is that it will take a culture change that people won’t want to do until it is forced in their faces. We used to have a much more circular economy, where people reused and rewashed everything, but we have been indoctrinated into a convenience culture, even if it then causes us more inconvenience.”

Dealing with trash is “gross problem”, Gallagher acknowledged. “But we need a much deeper conversation about it rather than continuously pushing it to the side because it’s uncomfortable and it confronts our human desire for comfort and our laziness,” she added.

The municipal government of New York City has pointed to recent efforts to reduce its waste, such as the pickup and composting of organic matter, which makes up around a third of what is left as trash in the city.

Yet New York City residents still create around 12,000 tons of trash a day and it will need to go somewhere. The city does not send residential trash to Seneca Meadows – although some private contractors do – but will be sending it further and further from the city, which has not hosted its own waste for several decades.

“As capacity continues to shrink in the region, we will likely export trash to further locations,” said a spokesman for the city’s sanitation department. “Our commitment to rail export makes this much easier than trucking.”

Yvonne Taylor, co-founder of Seneca Lake Guardian environmental group, stressed she didn’t want other communities to suffer living near growing landfills like hers had.

Residents routinely text her to say that they have had to remove their children from the nearby school because the smell had sickened them, or of ruined outdoor birthday parties and other gatherings, she said. Pitifer, of Waterloo Containers, said the company has had to install filtration equipment to help employees deal with the overpowering stench of the landfill.

“We don’t need to use plastic grocery bags, we don’t need to use plastic toothbrushes, toothpaste, shampoo bottles, and laundry detergent bottles – all of those things can be packaged in other materials that don’t wind up in a landfill,” said Taylor.…

T he US Federal Aviation Administration’s decision to ground all flights on Friday threw airports and travel plans into chaos across the country, as passengers on planes and in airport terminals were suddenly thrust into limbo.

At New York’s John F Kennedy airport, passengers found their travel plans abruptly cancelled – some even after they’d boarded.

Steve Honberger, heading home to Portland, Oregon, with his wife and daughter, said he’d been on a plane about to take off when the shutdown was announced.

“They didn’t seem to know what’s happening, and they wanted to hold off as long as possible,” Honberger said. The plane sat at the gate for an hour and 40 minutes.

Many still thought it worth showing up despite the uncertainty of when flights would resume. Rashid Kahn, heading for Miami, said he’d “heard about the ground stop on the news, but the airline said we might take off 10 or 11pm”.

Tom Rolenaitis, returning a Shiba Inu show dog named Tsuki to Finland, said it was frustrating. “It’s cutting into a three-day trip and I have to get him back to his owner. We have no idea what’s happening.”

A flight attendant headed for Barcelona, who declined to give his name, said he had been told his American Airlines flight would be slightly delayed and all incoming international flights were being allowed to land.

Another crew member from the flight said cheerfully: “Things happen. Hopefully it will all be resolved.”

As the day wore on, passengers on international flights began to be boarding, prompting applause to erupt at the gates. “It’s moving, so that’s good,” said an airline representative. “But only international is going.”

The FAA issued the nationwide ground stop on Friday afternoon, citing a communications problems at regional air traffic control centers, according to an FAA notice. Four hours later, FAA sent out an advisory lifting the stop.

“You can’t moan about this kind of thing ... it’s such a first-world problem,” said Laura, a woman who lives in New York and was heading for San Francisco when her JetBlue flight was grounded. She still hoped her flight would go. “That what I have to figure out,” she said, sitting on the floor of the terminal.

With the lifting of the ground stop, more chaos followed. “My flight was cancelled, then I go to a kiosk, put my information in and it says I’m leaving at 3am. Then I talk to the desk and they know nothing,” said Larson Welsh, heading to Las Vegas from Paris.

There have been 10,343 flight delays within, into or out of the US so far, according to the website FlightAware, and 1,479 cancellations. More than 1,000 aircraft were bound for US when the ground stop was announced, according to Flightradar24.

Only two national ground stops have previously been issued: on 11 September 2001, after the terrorist attack on the World Trade Center; and in January 2023, after a communications failure.

The ground stop also snarled the sports world, leaving NBA, NHL and college teams stranded as they tried to reach their destinations before a big weekend of games. It also was unclear whether referees, who typically fly to their assignments the day before games, would make it on time.

Back at JFK, travelers expressed frustration and resignation.

Honberger, meanwhile, tried to stay optimistic, saying: “There are people sitting on tarmac, so we count ourselves lucky and we were able to book ourselves a hotel for the night.”

A previously unseen family archive offers a glimpse into the Indian Nobel prize winner’s artistic process and personal relationships in his final years

I t’s easy to run out of words to describe Rabindranath Tagore. The first non-European to win the Nobel prize in literature, Tagore was a Bengali poet, musician, novelist, philosopher, songwriter, painter, humanist and educator.

Born in 1861, Tagore left an indelible mark on the subcontinent’s literature, music, education and art. Among his enduring legacies are the national anthems of India and Bangladesh.

As Nobel laureate economist Amartya Sen once wrote , Tagore was “a towering figure in the millennium-old literature of Bengal”, whose songs resonate across eastern India and Bangladesh, while his ideas on education, nationalism and freedom of the mind remain relevant today.

Yet his work also made a deep impression on the literary world far beyond the shores of India. WB Yeats is said to have described Tagore as “greater than any of us”. Gitanjali, the collection of poems that won Tagore the Nobel prize that same year, was praised by the committee for its “profoundly sensitive, fresh and beautiful verse”. Tagore’s English translation was published in London that March and reprinted 10 times by the time the prize was announced in November.

Tagore’s life and works have, of course, been well documented, but a collection of material preserved in a private family archive is now being brought into public view for the first time at an exhibition by Christie’s, opening in Mumbai this month. The archive draws from Tagore’s visits to the family home of his protege, Maitreyi Devi, in the bucolic village of Mungpoo in Darjeeling between 1938 and 1940. He died in 1941.

The collection on display – artworks, manuscripts, letters, photographs and personal effects – offers an intimate glimpse into Tagore’s creative process and personal world in his final years.

I spoke to the exhibition curator, Nishad Avari, head of south Asian modern and contemporary art at Christie’s, about the stories behind the archive.

One instructive document Avari points to is a manuscript from 1940. It appears to be a draft of Tagore’s memoir Chelebela or My Boyhood Days, in which he reflects on his life – from growing up in a large family in Calcutta (modern-day Kolkata) to the rapidly changing world ushered in by electricity and the motorcar.

For Avari, what stood out was how the ideas in the document echoed the educational philosophy Tagore put into practice in Santiniketan (or Abode of Peace), the experimental school he set up about 100 miles from the state capital.

“He speaks about how education is like being in prison and that it should be open and free … about the idea of wonder and even fear as inspiring creativity,” Avari told me.

“That’s a direct relationship to Santiniketan and the open model of the school where people sat under trees with their gurus and learned in the open. Education didn’t feel like a restriction, prison or imposition,” he added.

Avari points to another detail that makes this particular document valuable. Of the 10 complete manuscripts in the exhibition, it is the only one dictated to Devi, whose father was a close friend of Tagore’s. For Avari, this speaks to their close relationship and the trust he placed in her.

“If you look at the collection as a whole, she has copies of almost every single one of his publications signed to her by him,” he says. The collection includes hundreds of letters, too: first between Tagore and her father, and later between Tagore and Devi herself.

There are doodles among corrections, Avari explains, which show how his literary practice fed into his artistic practice. Alongside the manuscripts and correspondence are vintage photographs and personal effects, including a kurta and a lungi that Tagore left behind at the family home.

Among the artworks in the collection is a portrait of Devi, particularly notable because Tagore’s figure studies were not generally attributed to specific individuals in the way that portraits by his nephews, Abanindranath and Gaganendranath, often were, Avari said. There is also a landscape depicting the forests of Mungpoo, which Tagore embraced as a retreat.

On the international art market, Tagore’s paintings command significant prices. This year, Sotheby’s sold one of his watercolours for £1.02m (Rs 12.97 crore), nearly four times its low estimate.

Institutions such as Visva-Bharati in Santiniketan and the National Gallery of Modern Art hold much of Tagore’s archival materials, making the discovery of a private archive particularly rare.

He hopes that making these materials public will offer historians, scholars and admirers alike additional perspectives on Tagore. “We hope to add to the understanding of the artist, their career, and in this case, of course, our understanding of the man beyond his art as well.”

Rabindranath Tagore and Mungpoo runs between 10 November and 18 December at Christie’s space in south Mumbai.

Paul Mackenzie convicted over deaths of children and one adult after followers were ordered to starve themselves and their families

The leader of a Kenyan doomsday sect has been sentenced to 200 years in prison for the murders of 190 children and one adult in one of the world’s worst cult disasters in recent history.

The sentence, comprising 100 years for murder by starvation and 100 years by direct homicide, came two weeks after the court in Kenya’s coastal city of Mombasa found the cult leader guilty of the crimes.

Prosecutors said Paul Mackenzie and his Good News International church ran ​a Christian doomsday sect whose members were ordered to starve themselves and their children to death to go to heaven before the world ended.

His accomplices threatened and beat victims to ensure they followed his orders. The emaciated bodies were found scattered in shallow graves and dumped in latrines. Some had been buried alive.

Mackenzie was arrested in 2023 after police received a tipoff, and weeks later authorities began uncovering bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola forest near the coast in south-eastern Kenya.

In total, more than 400 bodies have been recovered. Many were severely decomposed and only 26 could be identified.

Mackenzie denied murder charges, saying he did not force the victims to starve, but the court rejected that argument.

The Shakahola tragedy has gripped Kenya since the discovery of mass graves in the forest more than three years ago.

It raised questions about how Mackenzie was able to continue operating despite being on the radar of the authorities since 2017, when police searched his premises.

In 2019, authorities shut down Mackenzie’s church and he relocated ‌to the Shakahola forest, police said.

The case has also led to calls for tougher oversight of churches and other religious organisations in a country where religious faith plays a prominent role in public life.

Mackenzie, a former taxi driver, forbade cult members from sending their children to school and from going to hospital when they were ill, describing such institutions as satanic.

Cult members lived in makeshift homes of polythene sheeting and thatch that Mackenzie divided into areas with biblical names such as Jerusalem and Judea.

The plight of his followers began ​to emerge in March 2023, when a man told ​police his brother and wife had starved their children ​to death in the forest on Mackenzie’s orders.

Mackenzie was arrested but released on bail, after which relatives said he brought forward the date ​on which he told his followers the ‌world would end. Police rearrested him and ​started combing through the forest more systematically and began exhuming mass graves.

Last month’s judgment covered 191 deaths while investigations into more than 200 other deaths are continuing.

Justice Diana Kavedza-Mochache said in a hearing lasting more than eight hours that in some cases children were isolated and denied food while their parents watched.

Mackenzie faces other charges over the forest deaths, including those of terrorism , which he has denied.

Prosecutors said that while he was in detention he also directed the deaths of 52 people in Kwa Binzaro village, about 18 miles from Shakahola. Mackenzie has pleaded not guilty in that case.

President orders prompt investigation after one train derails in collision in al-Ayyat about 30 miles from Cairo

From the assassinations of her husband and mother-in-law to press stonewalling under Modi, Belonging offers an insider’s account of India’s political evolution

F ew love stories have been as closely entwined with a nation’s history as that of Sonia and Rajiv Gandhi. The former’s much-awaited political memoir, Belonging, offers a strikingly candid account of her journey from a small town in Italy to the highest echelons of power in India – all for love, she says.

The veteran Congress party leader has been fiercely protective of her personal world. In Belonging, she opens up for the first time about the extraordinary twists and turns of a life that has largely unfolded in full public view. (The Guardian’s Hannah Ellis-Petersen has a rare in-person interview with Gandhi , and you can read an excerpt from the book here .)

Belonging, published today, contains moving glimpses of Gandhi’s private grief. She writes about the loss of her first child, who died shortly after birth, and the chilling discovery of grenades in a room of their house after Operation Blue Star, the 1984 military operation against Sikh separatists at the Golden Temple in Amritsar. She also provides a ringside view of several turbulent chapters in Indian politics, not least the violent assassinations of her mother-in-law, Indira Gandhi , in 1984 and her husband, Rajiv, in 1991.

Her book also revisits some of the darker episodes that have dogged the Gandhi family and the Congress party, including Indira’s imposition of the Emergency in June 1975, a 21-month period during which civil liberties were suspended, political opponents were jailed and the press was gagged, which caused fear and dismay across the country. In Gandhi’s account, italso caused a rift within the family.

Ultimately, Gandhi’s memoir is a vivid record of six decades of India’s political transformation from the Congress-dominated secular republic she moved to in 1968 until today, when Hindu nationalism has become the dominant political force under Narendra Modi .

Here are five key takeaways from her memoir and what they reveal about the state of Indian politics today.

Gandhi has had no real contact with Modi for the last 12 years

Gandhi’s account offers a glimpse of how deep the political polarisation runs in Indian politics today. In one revealing passage, Gandhi writes that she has had “practically no real contact” with Modi in the 12 years he has led the nation. In fact, at times when the two have been in the same rooms, such as the speaker’s small chamber, Modi “tends to look away, avoiding eye contact”, she says. On occasion, she adds, he has asked briefly about her health after a hospital stay.

For her, this breakdown is a departure from the past, when leaders on opposing sides of the aisle “would treat one another with cordiality”. After the 2001 terror attack on parliament, Gandhi immediately called then-BJP prime minister AB Vajpayee to enquire about his safety, a gesture he appreciated.

Gandhi sees an increasingly authoritarian style of politics, in which those in power seek to “belittle and torment” opponents. For years, Gandhi’s son, Rahul, has been the subject of BJP’s ridicule, which calls him Pappu, a derisive term intended to portray him as inexperienced and naive. She adds that similar things are happening elsewhere in the world, an observation that can be read in the context of US President Donald Trump’s use of personal insults and ridicule against opponents .

It’s lonely at the top for India’s female politicians

India has an illustrious history of women occupying top leadership positions, long before many other democracies. But their rise has often come at a cost – that of loneliness in navigating a male-dominated political world.

In the book, Gandhi describes a 2012 conversation with Hillary Clinton on the countrys’ female leaders and their backgrounds. In her recollections of Indira, she shares that, despite wielding authority, Indira could feel besieged and profoundly alone, and this was particularly acute, Gandhi writes, in the months leading up to the declaration of the Emergency by her mother-in-law.

Gandhi also writes of her own isolation, including when she decided to take on the leadership of the Congress out of a sense of duty to her family’s political legacy.

Those in power are increasingly stonewalling the press

Among the many ways in which Gandhi charts the erosion of India’s democratic conventions in Belonging, one particularly telling shift is the changed relationship between the media and those in power. She recalls a time when journalists had opportunities to question prime ministers directly.

In 12 years in power, Modi has not addressed a single press conference on his own. He has sat in on one press briefing at the conclusion of an election campaign, and appeared alongside US presidents at joint press encounters after bilateral meetings, where they took questions from the press. Modi has consistently avoided facing journalists in an open forum, and his media interactions have largely been one-on-one interviews with sympathetic, pro-government news anchors or in one much publicised exchange with a Bollywood actor who asked him how he liked to eat mangoes .

The book’s publication has brought renewed attention to concerns about the space for free expression in contemporary India, and the extent to which apprehensions about repercussions may influence what can be said, written and published.

Penguin Random House India was to publish Gandhi’s memoir but withdrew from the project in August. Gandhi told the Guardian that it was “uneasy in general with the criticism of the government” and said it had dropped the book after she declined certain suggested edits. Penguin has disputed her account, saying that the suggestion it decided not to publish the book because of refused editorial changes “does not accurately reflect the circumstances”.…

Hasina fled to India in 2024 after mass uprising. She faces death penalty upon return

Sheikh Hasina is “confident” she will return to Bangladesh in December, according to exiled members of her party, after the disgraced former prime minister of Bangladesh applied for a fresh passport this week.

Hasina has been living in self-imposed exile since August 2024 when she was toppled from power by a mass uprising against her authoritarian rule. She fled over the border to India, where she has since been allowed to live freely in Delhi.

Last November, a tribunal in Bangladesh found Hasina guilty of crimes against humanity and sentenced her to death over her deadly crackdown on a student uprising that left an estimated 1,400 people dead.

Her return to Bangladesh is likely to be disruptive for the country where Hasina’s party, Awami League, is still banned and thousands of its members are in jail. Should she be allowed to return, she is likely to be arrested immediately.

Hasina first raised the prospect of going back to Bangladesh in August. Speaking to the Guardian this week, several exiled Awami League leaders also living in India confirmed that Hasina was serious and “confident” about returning by next month. They confirmed that several other party figures had returned to the country in anticipation.

On Monday, a UK lawyer acting on behalf of Hasina, wrote to the Bangladesh high commission requesting a new passport and national identity card to be issued “in a timely fashion”, in a letter seen by the Guardian.

“The reason our leader Sheikh Hasina has applied for a passport is that she genuinely wants to return,” said a party leader based in the Indian city of Kolkata, who spoke on condition of anonymity because he is not authorised to speak to the media on the party’s behalf.

Hasina has rejected the charges of mass murder and crimes against humanity and claimed the tribunal who convicted her was illegitimate. “She is confident about her return, which is why she has applied for a new passport and a national identity card. If the authorities do not issue her a passport, she will apply for a travel pass to make her return to Bangladesh possible,” said the Awami League leader.

Since Hasina’s conviction, Bangladesh government has put pressure on the Indian authorities to extradite the former prime minister. However, the Indian government – which was very close to Hasina while she was in power – has ignored the demands, straining ties between the two countries.

This week, the Bangladesh government have said that as a “terrorist”, Hasina will only be allowed to return under an “acceptable prisoner exchange” under the India-Bangladesh extradition treaty. The chief prosecutor of the tribunal who sentenced Hasina condemned her announcement to return as a “nothing but a political stunt”.

Despite her conviction and the banning of her party, Hasina still commands significant popularity among the thousands of Awami League cadre still in Bangladesh, many who have been driven underground.

Analysts believe her decision to return, despite the risk of arrest, is driven by an attempt to revive her support base and destabilise the newly-elected government, led by prime minister Tarique Rahman. They were brought to power after in February in Bangladesh’s first democratic election in decades.

Since then, the government has struggled with inflation and recent protests that shut down garment factories, which Awami League hopes to use to its political advantage.

Another Awami League leader said all those in exile intended to follow Hasina back to Bangladesh, despite the threat of arrest and jail. Many of those who were close to Hasina over her 15 years in power have faced severe criminal charges since the fall of her government and have been given lengthy prison sentences in absentia.

“All of us are planning to go back. Some of us have been sentenced in absentia by kangaroo courts, and we know we will be jailed. But we are ready to face the consequences and return to our own people. We will fight this politically,” said the senior leader, who is also based in India.

Some senior party figures have already gone back in recent months, including former MP Mustaque Ahmed Ruhi. Ruhi was immediately arrested by police after returning in September and faces prosecution over an alleged murder committed during the 2024 uprising.

“There are serious threats and dangers, but our cadres and leaders are confident and prepared to return to our people,” the leader said.

During their years in exile, Awami League leaders have continued to meet in Kolkata, where many of them are living, and are routinely summoned to Delhi to meet Hasina.

Speaking over email this week, Hasina told the Associated Press she affirmed her decision to go back. “If death is my destiny, I would rather die on the soil of my own country, among my own people,” she said.

Seven-time F1 world champion tours border area and logistics warehouses operated by Egyptian Red Crescent

Tomás Beltrán was shot dead amid gang warfare that has turned Latin American country into one of its most violent

Tomás Beltrán was manoeuvring his car into his garage on Sunday night when the Ecuadorian journalist was shot dead.

Beltrán ran a Facebook page with news about Calceta, a small city in the province of Manabí, whose Pacific coastline has made it a key flashpoint in the gang warfare over drug trafficking routes that has transformed one of Latin America’s safest countries into one of its most violent .

Police and the public prosecutor’s office have not said much about the case, and little was known about the killers except that they were armed and then fled the scene. It was also unclear whether the crime was linked to Beltrán’s work, though he had previously reported allegations of corruption involving local authorities.

Regardless, many press freedom groups already cite his murder as the latest example of how conditions for journalists have deteriorated dramatically in Ecuador. Six journalists were killed in the country last year alone.

Artur Romeu, Reporters Without Borders’ Latin America director, said in a statement that months ago Beltrán had told the organisation “about his fears and the threats he was receiving”.

“We took part in efforts to get him to safety,” he said, adding that Beltrán had been placed in a protection programme run by the public prosecutor’s office, although it was not known whether that protection was still in place when he was killed.

“Reporters Without Borders calls on the public prosecutor’s office to investigate as a priority whether there is a link to his journalistic work, identify any possible masterminds and protect his family and colleagues,” said Romeu.

The Ecuadorian civil society organisation Fundación Periodistas Sin Cadenas (FPSC) reported that at least 19 journalists have had to go into exile since gang violence exploded in 2023. Although Ecuador does not produce cocaine like neighbouring Colombia and Peru, it has become a major trafficking hub , particularly through the Pacific.

Journalists have received death threats with photographs of their homes and details of their routines and families.

“Practising journalism in Ecuador is now an extremely high-risk job,” said María Fernanda Almeida, a project coordinator at FPSC, adding that all of last year’s killings of journalists “remain completely unpunished”.

“And one of the many terrible effects of this violence is self-censorship: at least in the coastal provinces, colleagues no longer want to report on violence,” she added.

Almeida said another problem for journalists has been the stance of the government of the far-right president Daniel Noboa, who has responded to the surge in crime with a controversial “iron-fist” approach to the gangs, repeatedly declaring states of emergency and expanding the role of the armed forces in measures that have been widely criticised by human rights groups.

While covering military operations, reporters have had their phones confiscated , a search warrant was executed at a reporter’s home and a journalist was threatened by soldiers simply for filming them stopping university students.

There have also been several reports that Noboa, one of US president Donald Trump’s key allies in Latin America, has pressured media organisations to dismiss journalists critical of him, including the columnist Roberto Aguilar, who said he was fired from the newspaper Diario Expreso after the government reportedly threatened private advertisers with audits if they continued advertising with the outlet.

Noboa’s administration did not respond to requests for comment.

“I don’t think there is complete freedom of expression in Ecuador today,” said Almeida. “And that is very worrying because the more violence and silencing there is, the more journalism is needed.”

Leonardo Bertulazzi, 74, awaiting extradition to Italy, reportedly used harness to flee custody

A 74-year-old former member of Italy ’s radical Marxist group the Red Brigades has escaped from house arrest in Argentina , the country’s security ministry confirmed on Wednesday, after he reportedly hid his ankle monitor inside a tube of pork and lowered himself from a fifth-floor balcony.

Authorities placed Leonardo Bertulazzi under house arrest in Buenos Aires in 2024, prior to his extradition to Italy to serve a 27-year prison sentence. He had received the sentence in 1987 for joining a subversive association and belonging to an armed group.

After years on the run, Bertulazzi was first arrested by Argentine authorities in 2002. He was freed a few months later and secured refugee status in 2004, but was arrested again in 2024 after it was revoked.

On Wednesday, Argentina’s security ministry offered a $13,000 reward for information leading to Bertulazzi’s recapture after he slipped out of detention.

The fugitive held a senior position in the Red Brigades, a radical Marxist organization responsible for attacks from 1969 to 1980, dubbed Italy’s “Years of Lead”. The group most notoriously kidnapped and assassinated former prime minister Aldo Moro in 1978.

Security footage showed Bertulazzi dropping from a building into a public road as cars drove past.

A detective tracking the former member of the Red Brigades reportedly told La Nación that Bertulazzi rappelled down from the fifth floor using a harness.

“First, he removed his electronic ankle monitor and placed it in a tube filled with pork, along with a blood pressure monitor to maintain the temperature. He then climbed on to a roof and, using a rope, lowered himself five meters until he jumped onto a vacant lot behind the building where he lived, and then scaled a metal gate to reach the street,” the detective said, according to the publication.

The footage, which indicated the time was 6.01am on 10 November, showed a possibly shaken Bertulazzi sitting down to rest for a few moments.

Police noticed his ankle monitor had stopped transmitting movement data and headed to the house, where they found the device discarded and Bertulazzi nowhere to be found.

Argentina approved his extradition to Italy in July 2025 after the country’s supreme court rejected a final appeal.

Capture of man from Java follows reports that hundreds are being recruited from the south-east Asian country as Moscow seeks to boost its war effort

Ukraine says it has captured its first Indonesian prisoner of war, amid what it says is a spike in recruitment by Russia from the south-east Asian nation.

The 49-year-old man from Java was taken to Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region to take part in a Russian assault, but managed to reach Ukrainian-held territory after the group came under drone attack, according to Ukraine’s state-run I Want to Live project. He was then captured by the Ukrainians.

According to the project, some 283 Indonesians were recruited in the first nine months of this year to fight for Russia against Ukraine. It said recruitment from Indonesia was no more than 10 in the previous three years.

The Russian embassy in Jakarta did not immediately respond to questions about the alleged recruitment effort but it is not the first time Russia has sought foreign mercenaries for its war effort.

In February, Kenya’s intelligence services reported that more than 1,000 Kenyans had been lured to fight for Russia.

A growing number of people from African countries – including Kenya, Uganda and South Africa – and elsewhere have been lured to the frontline as Russia seeks help to sustain its more than four-year war after invading Ukraine in February 2022.

This month Jakarta urged Moscow to ensure no Indonesians were drafted into its military, following the reported death in October of an Indonesian national serving with the military.

Indonesian foreign ministry spokesperson Yvonne Mewengkang said: “The Indonesian government asked the Russian government to take all necessary steps to ensure that no Indonesians will be recruited into the Russian military or any other military-related position in Russia through any avenues.”

Indonesia, she added, was particularly concerned about recruitment practices that could constitute human trafficking.

Days later, Indonesian police said they had identified a human trafficking syndicate targeting its nationals that used social media and messaging apps to recruit victims.

The posts promised lucrative jobs in logistics, border security and defence construction, but after the applicants travelled to Russia they were directed to sign contracts to serve as mercenaries, with some deployed to conflict zones, police said.

The ‘I Want to Live’ governmental initiative was established in September 2022 by the coordination headquarters for Prisoners of War with support from Ukraine defence ministry and defence intelligence (HUR).

It was designed to allow active-duty troops, including Russian servicemen and foreign nationals recruited into the Russian military, to safely surrender and exit the battlefield.

Statement is rare instance of a prominent Jewish political leader taking a strong stand in defence of Arab Israelis

Israeli prime ministerial hopeful Gadi Eisenkot accused caretaker premier Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday of fuelling a “racist” campaign against the country’s Arab minority, after he sought to delegitimise the community’s lawmakers by linking them to Hamas.

Two Arab-majority parties, Ra’am and the Joint List, secured a combined 19 seats in last month’s election, winning nearly a sixth of the 120-seat parliament and potentially emerging as kingmakers in efforts by Eisenkot to form a government.

“Arab citizens of Israel are an integral part of the Israeli story,” Eisenkot wrote on X on Friday.

“They have been subjected to a racist and aggressive campaign of delegitimisation, fuelled by the outgoing prime minister and those around him for political purposes,” he added.

“The attempt to marginalise them and vilify them collectively is a profound violation of the principles of civic responsibility.”

Netanyahu and his allies have repeatedly criticised leaders of Arab parties for refusing to describe Hamas as a “terror group” after its unprecedented 7 October 2023 attack on Israel.

All leaders of Arab parties have condemned the attack, in which Arab Israelis – descendants of Palestinians who remained in what became Israel in 1948 – were also among those killed.

Netanyahu has also repeatedly alleged electoral fraud by Arab-majority parties, but electoral authorities have rejected the claims.

In a speech, Netanyahu lamented that the two Arab lists refused to recognise Israel as a Jewish state, although Ra’am’s leader, Mansour Abbas, has done so in the past.

He further claimed that they sought to establish either an “Islamic state” or a “nationalist Palestinian state”.

During the same ceremony, the national security minister, Itamar Ben Gvir, heckled Joint List’s leader, Yousef Jabareen, during his oath of allegiance, accusing him of having “pledged allegiance to Hamas”.

“It is entirely legitimate to disagree with representatives of the Arab parties, even to strongly disapprove of some of them. But it is neither legitimate nor acceptable to malign an entire community, and I will not allow it,” Eisenkot said.

President Isaac Herzog tasked Eisenkot with forming a new government on Sunday after consultations in which a majority of political parties, including the two Arab lists, recommended him for the role.

But one of Eisenkot’s rightwing allies, Avigdor Lieberman, has said he will back out of the coalition if Arab Israelis are part of it.

Nvidia’s supply-chain emissions have grown 725 percent since 2020, according to an analysis of the company’s public disclosures by research analyst Ketan Joshi and several environmental organizations, including Greenpeace and Climate Action Against Disinformation, published in September. Supply chain emissions the company disclosed for fiscal year 2026 reached around 10.7 million metric tons of CO2, according to Nvidia’s latest sustainability report .

Joshi and his co-authors approximated how much greenhouse gas pollution comes from the use of chips the company sells, a category Nvidia doesn’t include in its sustainability reports. Those emissions could have reached 21 million metric tons in 2025, according to the report, based on estimated chip power consumption. That level of pollution puts Nvidia on par with Russia’s state-owned coal company, according to Joshi .

Those “indirect” emissions — from its supply chain and the use of its products — make up the bulk of Nvidia’s climate impact. The carbon footprint of facilities Nvidia actually owns and operates looks much smaller in comparison because Nvidia designs chips that other companies like TSMC then manufacture . Greenhouse gas emissions coming directly from Nvidia-operated facilities and vehicles only reached 9,822 metric tons in fiscal year 2026, the company’s sustainability report shows. And in 2025, the company reached a goal of matching 100 percent of its facilities’ electricity use with clean energy purchases.

Greenpeace wants Nvidia to extend that goal to its entire manufacturing supply chain. Listing the details of everything for sale everywhere is meant to make Amazon more useful than Reddit for people and AI agents.﻿

Amazon has plans to build a vault of data on every product sold anywhere on the internet, even products Amazon doesn’t sell, and make the information available through its own site, according to Reuters . The project, called the “World Product Graph,” is meant to make it less likely that shoppers leave Amazon to do their product research on Reddit or Google, and make it more likely shoppers end up at Amazon even if they’re searching for a product sold elsewhere. The same goes for AI agents — if Amazon has the largest stockpile of shopping data, AI agents may rely on its index of products over others, so even people shopping with bots will end up on its pages.

Links to outside retailers’ products have already started popping up on Amazon through the “shop direct” feature it launched last year. The company also has its own AI shopping assistant , Alexa for Shopping, previously called Rufus. The World Product Graph project would also be aimed at fixing issues with the AI by providing it more data. According to Reuters , an internal Amazon document on the project says “Many Rufus answers are factually wrong or incomplete” and running users’ Amazon searches with the AI is expensive. Adding more data is reportedly supposed to make the system more accurate and able to use cheaper models.

Whether this actually ships is still up in the air. The internal document reportedly says the project “depends on discovering how brands organize their products on their own websites,” which could involve Amazon crawling other retailers’ sites. Reuters says it’s unclear “if or when this plan may be implemented,” but said the document on it included an October 1st, 2027 release date.

Amazon said in a statement to Reuters that “Draft, outdated documents often paint an incomplete picture and the existence of a brainstorming document such as this one doesn’t necessarily reflect our current plans.”
